It is scary because of the effect it has on students. I teach pre-GED level in a community college setting in the CUNY system. Many of my students in my classes are products of a failed public school system. Thus many of my students walk into my classroom the first day with a huge dark shadow of failure dogging their every effort. I am new to teaching, about two years now. It is a second career for me; I was, in another life, an education program coordinator. So I have much to learn about teaching.And although my heart is in the right place it has been a struggle for me to try to help my students overcome this heavy belief that they are failures, especially when it comes to math. Recently I was talking to a new colleague who just joined our staff this year, but who has been teaching for awhile. She was talking about the difficulty of teaching to so many different levels of ability in our classrooms. And she is right. We do have students with such a variety of strengths and ability who come from so many different backgrounds. So it is a dilemma how to catch the attention and interest of all. But I was horrified to hear her say that she grouped her students, that she felt it was the best way to teach to all skill levels. While I know that I lose many students (we all do in these programs) for whatever reasons and few finish out the semester, I do know that by the end of the semester I can look around my classroom and see all students working together. Yes my lesson planning and teaching are always a work in progress and I have so much room for improvement, but I almost cry to think of the adults in her classes who are assigned to their group and subtly told, this is it for you, I am confirming your negative sense of your abilities. I have a high proportion of perfectionist students in my class, so I have developed several ongoing procedures to model learning from mistakes, and to put mistakes in learning perspective. When I call on students attempting to answer a challenging question (and sometimes I cold call), I will sometimes make explicit that I am checking for understanding, or trying to evaluate where students are now in their thinking. Because it works for me, I also rhetorically ask \will the floor open and swallow him if he's wrong?\" or \"will anyone die if she makes a mistake?\" In addition, especially during math, I remind them to be watching carefully because I make frequent mistakes, or get confused. Often, if someone catches a mistake I'm making, I give them a point,and invite them up to show us their thinking. Occasionally, I'm not wrong, but the student works through a confusion (which others usually share). Similarly, students routinely come up to demonstrate how they got answers. Time permitting, we have people show all the different ways they arrived at the answer. Those who get different answers come up, partly so we can resolve the issue, figure out how and why different answers arose -- which one is \"right,\" and what error in thinking or calculation caused the mistake. Sometimes students can identify where another student has a confusion before I can, and explain it better, since they have already \"been there,\" and worked through the error."

One thing that has worked in my elementary school is the introduction of daily word problems.  Our administration believes that using math story problems in our classrooms can give every student a chance to develop understanding of basic math concepts.  This has been highly successful.  First, we introduce a real life situation based on our math objective.  We then have the students tell each other the story and what the specific task is.  We then have the students use unifix cubes, drawings, numerical representations of how they solve the problem, using at least one representation that can be put down on paper.  This lets all level of achievers to use whatever forum they want. When higher students finish, we give them the task to solve it another way and show their thinking. As students work individually, the teacher goes around and asks students what they are showing (how they are making sense of their thinking) and selects three students to present their strategies to the class.  These presentations are to be from simple to more complex so that all students can see/relate their thinking to another way of solving the problem.  This has been highly successful in our school practices and has shown us that all students can do math.  I found that at the end of doing this for an entire year, most if not all students were able to express their math thinking with ease and were more than eager to share and be presenters to the class.  I noticed doing daily math word problems also obliterated the anxiety that often accompanies such problems. We do not use ability grouping for math in my school.  Two years ago, in 3rd grade (which is the grade I teach) our administrator asked the 3rd grade team to split our students by ability for reading.  We did this for several reasons, but primarily because we had to document for RTI (Response to Intervention) for those students reading below grade level.  We used several tools to determine where to place children and the children were never told that they were being \grouped\", just that we were changing teachers for reading groups. [And, yes, some of them could figure out what we were doing.]  The groups were fluid, however, so that if a child made significant progress in reading ability, he or she was \"moved\" to another teacher (essentially another/higher group).  What we discovered was that those children who were so very low that they couldn't read was that once they were placed in a very small class, they began to participate more AND their reading difficulties became more obvious.  Why? Because suddenly those children could not disappear into the larger group.  They felt more at ease responding because they were in the same boat as everyone else at the reading table.  Most of those children made huge strides in their reading levels.As a teacher I noticed that even though we used several tools, some children were incorrectly placed. Your first equation is a good representation of the problem.  The goal now is to find out what 'x' is.  Your second equation doesn't get you any closer to that goal, nor the third.  In such a problem I tell students that we are trying to find out what x is, not what 4x is, or x + 2, but just x.  To do that we need some kind of an answer such as \x = .....\".  To get there we need to get x all by itself by using manipulations that maintain the sanctity of the equals sign.  This is where the creativity comes in -- the student can do whatever they want.  Some manipulations will get closer to the goal of \"x - ....\", some won't.  It doesn't matter how fast they get there.  Doing manipulations that don't help helps the student see what will and what won't help.  You could view this as making a mistake if the goal is to get to \"x = ...\" as quickly as possible.  This is where the learning comes in.  From your first equation, if the student was stuck, I'd point out there are an awful lot of x's there, is there a way to put them together."

I have tried all different types of grouping, and my favorite way is what I call A/B partners.  I change up these partners throughout the year - sometimes they are based on confidence, sometimes on types of thinkers (pictorial vs. abstract), sometimes it is just random.  I have tables in my room, so I have 3 sets of a/b partners at each table unless someone is absent of I have an odd numbered group, then there are 2 As and a B, or visa-versa.  With A/B partners I have the As explain something to the Bs, or the B's, to the As, and then often times the table group will then discuss as a group comparing their solutions and discussing things.  I've found that by having flexible groups, students don't feel like they are being pigeon holed into a particular group.  I've also found that sometimes students surprise me because they may work really well with a particular partner and they both really bring out the best thinking in one another.  Also, it allows students to work with different types of personalities, which is also a good life skill.  Therefore, I think grouping should be flexible and change often.

It's easier to grasp if you begin with simple numbers. For example, If I start with a piece of wood that is 12 inches long, how many 2-inch pieces can I get out of it? Answer: 6 pieces of wood, each 2-inches long. That's the same as 1 divided by 1/6.    If I start with a piece of wood that is 12 inches long, how many 3-inch pieces can I get? Answer: 4 pieces. That's 1 divided by 1/4.    If I start with a piece of wood that is 12 inches long, how many 6-inch pieces can I get? Answer: 2 pieces. That's 1 divided by 1/2.  So far, all these lengths (2,3,6) are factors of 12, so we get whole number answers. The number of pieces we get goes down as the length of the piece desired increases.   If I start with a piece of wood that is 12 inches long, how many 8-inch pieces can I get? Answer: 1 piece that is 8-inches plus one piece leftover that is 4 inches (half the desired length), or 1.5 8-inch pieces.  That's 1 divided by 2/3.

Students walk into our classroom with a load of stereotypes that they have gotten from a variety of sources. We can help them shed these stereotypes by challenging the student to do their best, giving positive feedback, and finding ways to address the learning issues each student faces. Being positive and building solid relationships with the students will help overcome these negative self-images.

Much of stereotyping is pre-conscious (or unconscious).  We make judgements before we know that we have.  Before we \think.\"  The judgements come out in gestures, inflections, subtle expressions that we are not even aware of.  It could be the student that we call on, the smile that we give.  If we are to counter these things of which we are not conscious in our interactions with others we must do so consciously and conscientiously.  We have to make a point to compensate.For me I find this easier to do with young kids than with adults sometimes.  When it is a parent about my age that I am working with I feel that I more easily slip.  thoughts will pop into my head and I will think, \"where did that come from?\"  Or with  young adults I often do the same.  Quick judgements can be very accurate, but we need to also question them reflectively and ensure that we are not perpetuating negative typing.We will never completely get rid of stereotypes.  Our mind sorts automatically to create quick judgements of people.  It is how we have evolved.  However, we know that many of these can be negative (and completely inaccurate), and as educators we need to confront these in ourselves (even if we would like to deny that they exist) and ensure that we treat each student with dignity."

One thing I've read about is that Support classes find unusual success when they pre-teach the material, rather than re-teach the material already covered. Think about it this way, when you use Support primarily to re-teach, you're admitting to the students that they're slower, that they're not as smart. Many of them are willing to take the Support Class because they want the extra assistance, but it is a subtle acknowledgement that they aren't \smart.\" When you pre-teach the material, you're decreasing the cognitive load that the students will go through on the day of class. Instead of \"Factoring?!? What does that word mean?\", they've practiced the word in resource class, and perhaps did some 4th-grade multiplication/factorization review and started the basics. Now, when they're in a group with high and low kids, the kids from the Support class have background knowledge to contribute. They're smart! They also will be able to follow along better with the lectured that's designed for-the-middle, because the very basics were covered the day before in Support class. And, the kids who traditionally get rewarded for having the background knowledge (the hand-raising volunteer types) have to step up their game because they suddenly have a lot more competition for teacher's pet. I don't remember what study it was that showed this effect, but it's definitely something to look into. It makes much better use of time than having a kid sit lost and confused through the difficult material, and then handing them easier work the next day in Support class. It sends mixed messages as to what rigor level is expected, and it can mean that the main math class was a waste because the kid didn't feel comfortable with the word Factorization and thus 90 minutes of material went over his head. I also have seen the Support classes can turn into hand-holding classes where the steps are more and more broken down by the teacher who is \"assisting\" the student, whereas when the material is being pre-taught, the goal of the Support class is about growing your background knowledge on a topic up to a comfortable level, and it's becomes a safe place for asking questions you don't know, which will be helpful when you learn them \"for real\" tomorrow. Anyway, best of luck - hope this helped!"

This process has similarities to i^29  = i and other situations where certain groupings reproduce patterns.  Another example is \what is the last digit of 9^1000?\"  This problem produces an overflow error on most calculating devices, but we can solve by looking for a pattern within the last digit and then dividing the 1000 by the number of numbers in our pattern and applying the remainder.  So, what I'm trying to say here is that I thought that putting Vivian's method in the category of the distributive property was nice, but the distributive property may not have been what she was really thinking. When talking about mistakes being helpful for brain growth, there was little attention on what happens in the case of recalling information (and providing a correct answer) without making a mistake. It was almost implicit that what happened was \no growth\".I have a theory based on what I learned about neural networks. When training a  neural network, there are 2 activities, creating new connections and reinforcing \"good\" existing connections. This reinforcement was critical for producing a well trained network and it was what made occasional \"bad\" connections unimportant. Recall activity, if not conducive to growth, it may play a key role in this reinforcement portion and still be extremely important.Neural network learning curves are often modeled using a sigmoid function (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sigmoid_function), this describes the fact that initial learning is shallow, but after some reinforcement it gets to a point where the learning becomes much stronger very quickly (where the slope of the sigmoid becomes much steeper) and then it reaches saturation, where it takes a lot more effort to produce an improvement. The key may be in finding the right balance between growth and reinforcement. If we focus too much on reinforcement (which may be a problem in the current education systems) then we reach saturation point and simply get diminishing returns. When we're close to saturation, focusing on growth is likely to produce much better results, but I believe there is also risk if focusing too much on the growth mindset and not providing sufficient reinforcement.Of <nameRedac_<anon_screen_name_redacted>> this is very speculative, and based on extrapolation from research done for other purposes that may or may not apply here. In working with students on such problems I abandon the goal of representing the situation in one variable and let them use A, B, and C to start with. I don't see a need to use just one variable, and having 3 variables allows the students to keep the original problem in their head a little longer in working the problem. Jumping right to using 'x' to show the relationship between the three piles is too big a step.  So:  B = A + 2; C = 4A; A + B + C = 14.  Then I talk about the importance of the equals sign.  The equals sign is a like a balance scale.  The equals sign means you have the same amount of stuff on the left that you do on the right.  The equals sign means that the thing on the left (same amount of stuff as the right) can be substituted for the thing on the right anywhere it appears in this problem.  And vise versa -- the thing on the right can be substituted for the thing on the left anywhere it appears in the problem.  So in this case, you can substitute A + 2 for B anywhere it appears in this situation, and 4A for C anywhere it appears in this situation.  So A + B + C = 14 can become A + (A + 2) + (4A) = 14.  I will actually write out A + B + C = 14 with lots of space, and then erase the B and write \(A + 2)\" in its place; erase C and write \"(4A)\" in its place.  At this point I will point out we now have a mathematical representation of the problem of piles of rocks and how many is in each pile.  We check that this mathematical representation truly does represent the problem.  Then I ask them for a leap of faith -- to not think about the original problem, but just look at the equation.  Now there is one variable in the equation and let's find out what it is -- view it as a puzzle.  I let them do any manipulation they want to as long as that manipulation honors the equals sign.  We look at the result of each manipulation, asking does it make the equation look less complex -- always keeping in mind that at this point, the goal is to get to \"A = ...\" -- finding out what A is.  Once we have A, I have the student look back at the original problem and tell me what we've found out.  I ask have we answered the question originally asked?  If a single variable, such as x is used, it is easy to think the problem is solved once we find x.  But by using A, and looking back at the original problem, we find that we know A, but there is still more work to do to find B and C."

An analogy is learning to drive: You study a book of rules and regulations to pass a test for a learners permit, which is used to actually practice operating the vehicle. You then demonstrate highway and parking skills and are awarded a license. At that point, a marginal (knowledgable, yet unexperienced and potentially dangerous) driver joins all others. It is continued practice, full of trial and errors, that makes this person a more competent driver ... until old age begins reversing the process. In my school in Ontario, Canada we do the group work in the context of a three-part lesson (see work of Marian Small).  The group work is done after the first part of the lesson which activates knowledge the children already have.  For example, if I wish the children to use groups to count (Grade 1), then the intro will have them practicing skip counting by 5 or 2's etc.  Then they work in arbitrary groups which change every day.  I wish them to be exposed to many different methods of thinking.  We call this a three part lesson (the third part being a whole group review of the work of the students where they comment on the math).  I am sure others are using it.  At first everyone wants to work with the 'smart' person in the class, but over the course of the year that changes.  I had never thought about it before, but I think this goes a long way toward dispelling the myth that only some can learn math.  The students see that even the students who may struggle can come up with great strategies to overcome their own struggles and this inspires others to do the same.

As Jo stated the reasons for low achievement among tracked students, I couldn®t help but recall my experiences in tracked classes where all of these things happened.  Students who were clearly far above the others in terms of their understanding were not challenged at all because the class was taught to the middle and low-achieving students in the class.  The teacher had low expectations of students and often reminded me that we were constrained in what we could teach because they were ™the low kids.š  Students clearly picked up on this and began to have low expectations for themselves as well, not turning in work or completing assignments that they viewed as busywork (because they were!!).	I am currently reading Robyn Jackson®s book, ™Never Work Harder Than Your Students.š  In this book, Jackson discusses the idea of tracking using the analogy of jumping over a rope.  She explains it in the following way: suppose your goal is that students will be able to jump over a rope that is at least two feet off the ground.  If you set up a rope two feet off the ground exactly, the students who can do it immediately will have nothing to do once they jump over it once or twice, and the students who have trouble will continue to struggle with a static, repetitive task.  If you set the rope up seven feet off the ground, you run into the same problem, but this time you have more students struggling and receiving messages that they are ™not good enough.š  If, however, you set up a rope that is two feet off the ground at one end, and 10 feet off the ground at the other, students are able to grow and challenge themselves, no matter what their starting point.  The key with this is that regardless of their starting points, all students are at the very least exposed to the high expectations further down the rope.  Even the students who are working to jump over a two-foot-high rope can anticipate moving along the rope towards the 10-foot end.  It is this heterogeneous grouping, where students® starting points are respected but where all students are still exposed to a challenging environment regardless of their starting point, that leads to the best learning.

In my school we do not track at all (7th-12th)  However, everyone does not necessarily take calculus.  Students have no choice in their math through grade 10. In grades 11 & 12 they pick classes with guidance from their teachers.  The MA state standards and MCAS test says kids have to be able to solve quadratics.  I personally agree with the person above that I don't believe that to be a necessary skill.  Do all kids need advanced algebra...I don't think so, although my school takes pride in thinking that most of our kids will and should.  If we could take away some of the content expectation and focus on the mathematical thinking, we could more easily group heterogeneously.  When we track, we put kids on a fixed path that due to prerequisites, they can never veer from.  Kids can go down a level, but in math, it is hard to go up a level as usually math is tracked in such a way that kids in upper levels take courses a year early.  So if someone gets stronger in math as they age, they haven't had the prerequisites to move into the upper level without taking a make up course.  With heterogeneous grouping and playing with abilities within a class, all students have the same basic concepts but can develop them to different depths.  If a student better understands one concept over another, they can move more deeply into that concept and spend more time on the basics of another.  Their pacing varies over the course of the year.  The problem right now is that college counselors are pressuring kids to take calculus to be competitive for colleges.  I find myself fighting this constantly with the argument, that I'd rather have the student take a course more suited to their current development and do well, then to take a course that looks challenging on paper only to \fail\" or feel like they are failing. There is a top-down affect.  High schools want to prepare kids to be successful in college, middle school wants to prepare kids to be successful in high school, etc. But in doing so, we are not necessarily doing what is developmentally appropriate at each grade level.  We need to take their brains where they are and work within the developmental confines of them at that point.  Learning can't take place if the work is too easy OR too hard."

LINK stands for: L - Learning with manipulativesI - Independent workN - New mathK - Keep it up gamesThis is a very empowering program.  On Mondays, you preview the week.  Then half of the class is doing an extension of previous learning and/or a preassessment of a coming unit while the other half is doing Linking Leaders and Co-leaders, DISCOVERING how to play a new game that they can teach the others.  every day, they all write in their math journals about something they learned that was significant to them.  On Tuesday through Friday, the teacher presents 2-3 minilessons, meet with 2-3 groups, and students will go to a LINK.After analyzing the pre-assessments, the teacher divides the class into two seperate groupings.  The first is a mixed ability group that gets a mini lesson on the current whole group unit of study.  The students are strategically paired so that they have a partner to work with at the independent station, even though they will have different assignments, in case they have questions.  They have the same partner for at least one week.  All students are also grouped into similar ability groups, where the teacher can focus on a common area of need with each group.  There are 4 mixed groups, but only 3 similar ability groups, allowing for one extra session for the similar ability group with the most needs.  These groups are very fluid based on the assessing.  at the end of every lesson cycle (between and after the mixed ability groups and the similar ability groups), there is a check in session with all students at the carpet to talk about their experiences and strategies. There are so many enlightening things that Cathy displayed during her number talk. The first was that when she asked the students for answers to the question 25 x 29 and one student gave his answer, Cathy asked if anyone else had a different answer. That is good because some teachers might just start lecturing; however another student said her answer and the first student quickly realized his mistake. This leads into the next thing i noticed. Instead of going forward describing the right answer, Cathy wanted to follow through with how the first student got his incorrect answer. Afterward, cathy acknowledged that the question was hard, mentioned that his thought process was interesting and asked if other students made a similar mistake. I think that during the class discussion acknowledging the question was difficult is a huge deal, because it then makes it ok if someone got the question wrong. Cathy also called the students incorrect thought process \interesting\" which is much better than say words like \"wrong\" or \"incorrect\". Finally, Cathy engages the entire class again by asking if there were similar mistakes made. Later on in the number talk, Cathy asked if any of the students solved the problem in a completely different way and put those answers on the board. Lastly, one thing that stood out to me was when Cathy asked the students to express the different methods in drawings or equations, she asked the students to write on their desks with their fingers. This is a subtle point but it is allowing the students to bring the problem from the abstract word in their minds to the physical world, on the table. This is an important observation because sometimes students get lost in process of their mind and its better to have things written out or, in this case, air written so the students can \"see\" the problem better."

One way to group my students that I found to be effective for both quick learners and those who need more time to learn is that I pair these learners together.  So, there is one quick and one slower learner paired together.  Usually the quick learner has quickly completed the task, but because their partner is not able to solve it as quickly, it causes the quick learner to slow down, reprocess what was done, and then explain it to their partner.  Then the slower learner is able to hear how the problem was solved, talk it over with their partner, and try to solve in the same way, or perhaps in a different way.  Then both partners come up in front of the class and must each explain one portion of how they solved the problem.  This helps both my learners to do the work and feel responsible.  When they solve it incorrectly, it puts it back on both of them to work together, instead of feeling like they solved it incorrectly because they are in a \low\" group or incapable."

Q: At the same submaximal workload on an exercise bike before and after endurance training, you will use:A: The same amount of oxygen.The concept of a submax workload and oxygen consumption is tricky, and often students in our class at Stanford have trouble with it before it clicks. So know your confusion is in good company. Lets see if I can be helpful. The main point is this: **it requires the same amount of oxygen for your body to do a certain amount of work.** If that work is below the maximal capacity, we call it a submax workload. For example, I did a few months of cycling training to increase my aerobic fitness a year or so back as a part of a previous teaching project. We tested my VO2max by doing a progressive (increasing workload every few minutes) test on a stationary bike where I wore a mask that measured the oxygen I was using at Week 0, Week 5, and Week 10 of my training regimen. My VO2max increased across my 10 week training program because my body had optimized components of the fick equation, meaning that I could finish the test at a later stage where I cycled at higher watts of resistance. Lets say at Week 0 my maximum resistance at the end of the test was 250 watts, but at Week 10 it was 350 watts. Because of my training, I was becoming a better cyclist! Here is the point. Regardless of my training and assuming my cycling technique didn't change, at 150 watts (a light, submaximal workload), my body needed to consume the same amount of oxygen at Week 0 Week 5 and Week 10 to do 150 watts of work. The difference is, at the end of the training, my body could consume more oxygen, and 150 watts of a submaximal workload was easier because it was a lower percentage of my overall VO2max. -Staff

Immersion in a tepid bath had long been the accepted means, along with medication, of quickly reducing dangerously high fevers in infants and toddlers in the ED. The primary problem with this method was that the children/ infants usually responded to the immersion with heat generating behaviors such as vigorous flailing about in the water and nonstop crying. In an attempt to eliminate, or minimize this counterproductive behavior, we began to drape our little patients with wet towels and place a fan in front of them. This evaporative cooling method proved very successful. The infants and children usually remained calm and fever reduction occurred even more rapidly than with the immersion method. Also, with our patients in a calm state, it was easier to notice when they began to shiver, thus signaling when to stop the cooling measure. Another indirect benefit of the evaporative cooling method was that parents were more willing to do this at home, if necessary, because they were much less likely to have to deal with a screaming, stressed out infant.

Ah, the frequentist vs. bayesian interpretations of confidence intervals!Short answer: neither interpretations suggest a 95% probability of truth for the parameter.Long answer: read on.For the frequentist, there is only one true value for the parameter, which is hidden and we can only approximate based on theories like the Central Limit Theorem. Note that with each random sample set, we expect to get different confidence intervals. Hence, the 95% confidence interval for a parameter indicates that if we repeated the fitting using multiple (& infinite) number of random sample sets, 95% of confidence intervals produced would contain the true parameter. For the bayesian, the parameter (or its estimate) is random and has an associated probability distribution. The 95% **credible** interval communicates the level of belief the experimenter has of the parameter i.e. she is 95% sure of the parameter estimate. Note that it is a subjective belief as the interval is of the posterior distribution based on the experimenter's chosen prior. So, if you're not confused by now, you haven't understood it. Also, like linear regression, the nearest neighbor classifier can be used with either quantitative or qualitative responses and the result is easy to interpret. In addition, the nearest neighbor method can perform similarly or better than linear regression for both prediction and inference dependent on the true form of the function. Security Council Resolution 1325 was passed unanimously on 31 October 2000. It invited Secretary-General Kofi Annan to carry out a study on the impact of armed conflict on women and girls, the role of women in peace-building and the gender dimensions of peace processes and conflict resolution. The Security Council was concerned about civilians in armed conflict, particularly women and children, who constituted most of the victims and were increasingly targeted by armed elements. This in turn had an impact on the possibilities for peace and reconciliation. Women played an important role in the prevention and resolution of conflicts and therefore it was important that they were equally involved in the process of maintaining international peace and security. The Treaty provides an international standard for protecting and promoting women’s human rights and is often referred to as a “Bill of Rights” for women.The International Convention to Eliminate All Forms of Discrimination Against Women (CEDAW) enshrines these rights-and recognizes that women and girls often face challenges to realizing their rights specific to their gender. As such, CEDAW urges an equitable approach to human rights, recognizing the range of gender-specific human rights violations, ranging from sex slavery to maternal mortality to property and inheritance rights. CEDAW is an effective tool for women to advocate for their own rights and a standardized benchmark to which all countries should aspire. . It is the only international instrument that comprehensively addresses women’s rights within political, civil, cultural, economic, and social life. As of August 2009, 185 countries have ratified CEDAW. The United States is among a small minority of countries that have not yet ratified CEDAW, including Iran and Sudan. The United States has the dubious distinction of being the only country in the Western Hemisphere and the only industrialized democracy that has not ratified this treaty. The human rights approach is essential to women's health but it is a very difficult sell (so to speak) to policymakers and leaders in developing countries who are mainly interested in economic development. This is not an indictment on the character of these persons but rather comment on the assimilation of a human rights approach into local cultures. In many cases a woman's rights are viewed through a lens of economic development and the woman becomes a means to an end. Nations create work opportunities for women which are part time, unskilled, low paying, in hazardous environments or even create underemployment simply to meet international pressure to provide work. In the some cases of women's health may not be viewed a fulfillment of a right to access quality care but rather as a means of limiting associated to a social 'ills' or financial inconveniences. I think this is because the health issues of women are still viewed as the concerns of an 'other': concerns of persons outside the realm of concern and control of persons with power (more often male, older, non poor). Working in women's health requires advocacy which targets changes in cultural perceptions of women's issues. To a certain extent the domestic violence data showing women being more supportive of GBV is not surprising to me. In many (not all) situations where women are abused, there is an underlying culture of abuse as an acceptable form of social interaction and sanction which transcends women's issues. It is no coincidence that many of the societies which neglect women's issues also have problems stemming from cultural norms which have entrenched the either/or paradigm. The human rights approach must move beyond policy strategies and and conceptually isolated programmes to become cultural movements.    The success of the groups identified depends on their and their allies capacity to positively affect local cultures.

Great question John. I'll do my best to do a quick and dirty overview of metabolism in a short note. Basically, your body has access to three main energy systems to help you do work. 1) Immediate energy  (ATP, creatine-phosphate) 2) Short term energy (fast glycolysis) and 3) Long term energy (oxidative, or oxygen using, metabolism). Energy systems 1 and 2 can be done without oxygen, and system 3 needs oxygen. Your body is using some combination of these three energy systems at any given time, but will rely more heavily on a particular system depending on the situation. The general theme relevant here is that the body transitions from relying on oxidative metabolism to relying on non oxidative metabolism as exercise intensity increases. To make this a little more practical, \going anaerobic\" means higher intensity exercise. If you find yourself breathing heavily (even if its not for very long!), you are likely dipping in to nonoxidative metabolism aka \"going anaerobic\". -staff"

Hi Marilyn,Maximum heart rate (HRmax) is the fastest pace at which a heart can beat.  To find it, people perform a stress test (often walking or jogging on a treadmill that gets steeper and steeper until the person can't continue even with verbal encouragement--ideally the exercise lasts about 10 minutes).  The equation \220 - age\" or \"208 - 70% of age\" are just estimates, with age being the best single predictor of true HRmax.  All biological variables (e.g. like the HRmax of 1000 people) are distributed in a bell shaped curve.  The prediction equations provide the average or middle point of that curve.  Lots of people will be within 5 beats of the prediction, but it's common for someone to be 10 beats higher or lower than the prediction. $R^2$ measures the strength of your model's fit. The metric is bounded between 0 and 1. A $R^2 = 0$ means your model is no better than using the mean of y to make predictions. A $R^2 = 1$ means your model perfectly predicts y. Obviously, you want your model to have a high $R^2$. However, the $R^2$ in your training data set will often be overstated due to overfitting. So if you fit a model and see a $R^2 = 1$ be extremely skeptical. You should apply your model to an independent test data set to see if you get a similar $R^2$.$R^2 = frac{MSE_0 - MSE_f}{MSE_0}$where $MSE_0$ is the mean squared error where your prediction for every observation is just the mean of y; $MSE_f$ is the mean squared error of using your model to predict every observation. Using this formula, you can interpret $R^2$ as the relative improvement in prediction by using a model rather than using just the mean of y.

I thought of a way to explain it to myself that I'll post in case it helps someone else.  Suppose person A is transmitting letters of the alphabet to person B from far away.  The equipment at each end is effected by extreme temperatures and/or extreme humidity causing voltage drifts.  Therefore sometimes the letter received by B differs from the true one transmitted by A.  Similar to morse code only in my example errors are normally distributed around the true letter.  In other words, if the true letter is \O\", the most likely errors states are \"N\" and \"P\".  If B constructs 95% confidence intervals showing that the letter is between \"M\" and \"Q\", he CAN say that based on past experience he is 95% percent certain that he put his intervals on either side of the the true letter.  He CAN NOT say that the unknown letter has a 95% chance of being between \"M\" and \"Q\".  If the true letter, unknown to B, is \"O\", \"O\" is either between \"M\" and \"Q\" or it isn't.  \"O\" does not change its position in the alphabet randomly."

This is not a trivial question at all.  What you're describing is subsampling, and it's very similar to the bootstrap.  The bootstrap is conceptually simpler to implement because a bootstrap sample of size n is roughly as noisy relative to the original sample as the original sample is to the population.  Whereas for subsampling you have to decide on which k to use, then you'll often have to make a correction for the fact that your resamples are of different size than your original sample.On the other hand, a subsample of size k is an \honest-to-goodness\" sample of size k from the original population, so there are situations where the bootstrap is known to give you a wrong answer and subsampling (with the appropriate correction) gives you a right answer.  For example, bootstrapping would be a wrong way to estimate SD(Max(x_1,...,x_n)) (can you see why?).  Whereas subsampling could give you a correct estimate of SD(Max(x_1,...,x_k)) (if k is chosen small enough, obviously k=n is wrong).  Then you need to correct that somehow if you want an estimate of SD(Max(x_1,...,x_n))"

As many others have pointed out, the Millennium Development goals that relate directly to women’s education are Goals 2 and 3. These goals concretely address the need to improve both the access to education as well as the curriculums in schools across the globe. That said, I would argue that all remaining goals are dependent on educating girls. As we’ve read—both in From Outrage to Courage and New Lessons—the power of educated women is broad and diverse. Particularly based on the data presented in these readings, it’s easier to understand how Goals 1, 4, 5 and 6 are more directly related to the benefits of education. Educated women are more active economically, helping eradicate poverty. Educated women are marrying later, helping reduce child mortality. Educated women are having sex later, and in New Lessons, educated women are more likely to practice safer sex, thus combating HIV and AIDS. Goals 7 and 8 are a bit more tangential, but I don’t think it’s a stretch to state that with all 6 previous goals being accomplished, especially with a powerful force of educated women (and men), that we cannot succeed in those final goals.What I would also add to the conversation, as some have done, is that quality education is as critical as access to education (e.g. lasting literacy rates). I would also argue that when thinking about education, it's imperative to consider it in the broader human rights context. Are we addressing other barriers while also considering education? Small steps do need to be taken, but it's important we take those outside of a vacuum.

'boot(Xy, myfun, R=1000)' takes the dataframe Xy, the function myfun, and the number R, and estimates the standard error for the value of myfun.  The function myfun must be a function of a dataframe and an index vector.  Behind the scenes, 'boot' will randomly create R index vectors.  For each of the R index vectors (which we never see), 'boot' takes the dataframe, subsets it using that index vector, and computes the value of myfun.  At the end of this process there will be R different values for myfun.  'boot' then returns the standard deviation of these R numbers, and this standard deviation will be a good estimate of the standard error for the value of myfun if we could apply myfun to many different samples (which we can't because we have only the one).

In the article, “New Lessons: The Power of Educating Adolescent Girls,” Lloyd makes an important argument regarding the importance of non-formal education.  In developing countries, where young and adolescent girls do not fully attend formal or state-run schools, non-formal schools or education facilities have emerged.  These non-formal schools are run by NGOs, donors or local communities to provide children and adolescents access to an education that they may not otherwise have.  I was lucky enough to volunteer at an NGO-run non-formal school in Udaipur, India. The school was directed towards gypsy children whose families often moved or who could not afford to have children leave for a majority of the day to attend state-run schools.  Although state-run primary education in India is free, poor families often require their children, especially girls, to stay home and work instead of getting an education.  Non-formal schools offer the opportunity for these children to attend school because they are often run at hours that can accommodate the children’s work day.  The school I volunteered at ran from 2pm-5pm.  Attendance was taken everyday and children were encouraged to attend daily through incentives such as a daily healthy meal and through threat of not being allowed back if they missed more than a week of school.   I noticed that there were more girls than boys between the ages of 5-8, however it was extremely evident that more boys aged 9-13 attended than girls.  Non-formal education facilities, such as this school in Udaipur, are important for children who cannot access state-run schools.  However, these facilities also require the attention of the global community in order to encourage and facilitate the attendance of adolescent girls.  Through offering schooling at different times throughout the day and accommodating to the needs of these girls, improved access to education could be achieved.  I agree with Lloyd in her suggestion that surveys be conducted on attendance in non-formal schools as well as in her suggestion that the non-formal sector and formal sector should be well integrated.  Through the help of donors and volunteers,  the non-formal sector could enable young and adolescent girls to attend formal secondary and post-secondary institutions.

No,no, don't worry, it's not a convention :) it's just that for some examples they don't use field data, but simulated data from known distributions. I.e., they know exactly which are $pi_k$ and $f_k(x)$ for each $k$ , so they know which are all the terms in the Bayes theorem and they can exactly compute $P(Y=k|X=x)$ . Once you have this conditional probability law, then it's trivial to construct the Bayes classifier. But in real life you only get a sample of data from a population! You don't know which are the distributions that generated it. Sometimes, that's exactly one of the things you would like to find out! In the case of LDA, for example, you *assume* that the $f_k(x)$ are normal and share a common standard deviation, but you don't know for sure. Also, you have no idea which are the means $mu_k$ and standard deviation $sigma$ of these (assumed) normal distributions, and you don't know which are the $pi_k$. Of course you can *estimate* them from data, but you don't know for sure.By the way, one of the examples where LDA got so close to the Bayes Classifier was an example with two classes,where $f_1(x)$ and $f_2(x)$ were *chosen* to be normal with the same standard deviation. That's also a reason why LDA did so well :)

I think you are getting confused because the order of the parts of the formula changes between the first formula (the general statement of Bayes theorem, and the second formula (which shows the specific application for discriminant analysis). The two parts of the numerator of the right-hand side of the first equation are:1. The conditional probability of $X=x$ given that $Y=k$. In discriminant analysis, this is the probability density function of $X$ (but only for those values of $X$ for which the class is $k$). Since probability density functions are usually written $f(x)$, this has been written as $f_k(x)$. 2. The probability of $Y=k$: in discriminant analysis this is called the prior probability (it's the probability of an observation having class $k$ if you know nothing else about that observation). In discriminant analysis, the notation for this is $pi_k$. What's confusing here is that in the second formula on slide 20, the order of these two parts of the numerator is reversed ... this is because in maths it's more conventional to write a variable _before_ a function, not after it (ie $f_k(x)pi_k$ means the same but looks a bit less conventional). Cheyne Stokes respiration has central apnea as a component. The central apneas are due to low levels of CO2 and the faster component is due to higher CO2 levels (increased respirations to blow off CO2) . BiPAP settings can be adjusted (the 'spread' between the two pressures) to control how much CO2 is blown off during a breath - that is how it addresses the problem. For someone who has Cheyne Stokes respirations, bilevel is not the preferred mode of treatment. Adaptive Servo Ventilation looks at airway restriction (to address any obstructive apneas) and also looks at lung volumes (to address low volumes due to central apneas)and automatically adjusts the pressures accordingly. Incidentally, PAP treatment does not bypass sensory information- it changes the environment and thus, changes what the sensors perceive.

If you were to do normal bootstrapping with this, one bootstrap sample might have the data point for 4 May followed by the data point for 25 December followed by the data point for 15 March, and so on. In time series data, subsequent data points are often not entirely independent, so normal bootstrapping would mean losing these dependencies in the noise.To get around that problem at least a little, block bootstrapping groups data points into blocks (of equal size, ideally), and these blocks are then randomly recombined into bootstrap samples. For example, with a data set of one point per day, the block size could be 7, i.e. one week. A bootstrap sample might then have the data points for 27 February to 5 May, followed by the data points for 23 to 30 December, followed by the data points for 11 to 17 March, etc. Some dependencies are still lost (the data of 11 March follows that of 30 December, though it can't possibly depend on that), but the dependecies within blocks (of 12 March on 11 March, of 13 March on 11 and 12 March, etc.) are retained.

However, it does not at all take into account how x relates to the dependent variable y. ----------The advantage of PCA is that it can help to better visualize the dynamics of variability of the x variables, and that's often interesting by itself.----------As an example where PCA is often used in financial risk measurements. Imagine the x dimensions represent interest rates for loan tenors, so x1 is the rate for a one year loan, just making up some numbers, say 1%, x2 is the rate for a two year loan etc., and you write down the vector x as you observe those rates in the market today:----------x(today) = (%1, %1.5, %2, %4, %5)----------Now, in finance those vectors are called a 'yield-curve', one field of study is to record instances of it into a large matrix and observing how the curve changes over time. A PCA analysis would then be used to visualize the dynamics of the curve. For example the first two factors would possibly look like:----------F1 = (%5, %3, %2, %1, %1)F2 = (%5, %3, 0, -%2, -%1) ----------The first factor shows that the curve thens to shift up or down in parallel, but the short tenors are more volatile. The second factor represents a tilting, where the front goes opposite to the far end. The goal for those models is then to describe the curve dynamics entirely in terms of those factors.----------So going back to the original question, in my understanding PCA is more about the dynamics of the regressors and does less in terms of learning from the responses. As you approach the ball, he is pushing right and you are pushing left to try to reach the ball.  Your torso muscles are fully contracted as you push, but he is stronger, so he is causing them to lengthen while tensed as you are pushed off the ball.   What happens inside the muscle is that the little cross-bridges that are trying to contract can get damaged as they are stretched without the opportunity to release properly.  This can cause micro (or major) damage to the muscles tissue. Most of the time the result is minor, just some inflammation and soreness. 1. Prevention of mother-to-child HIV transmission (PMTCT) This type of intervention would provide medications, counseling, and support for HIV-positive mothers and mothers-to-be. Although there is a biomedical component as evidenced by the distribution of medications, it is also heavily reliant on working with health workers, community leaders, and change agents at the local level to educate women and men about ways to prevent mother-to-child HIV transmission. It is important that both women and men receive accurate information on PMTCT in order to foster a community of support around HIV-positive mothers and mothers-to-be. 2. Engaging boys and men as partnersThis second intervention works with small groups of boys and men to educate them about HIV/AIDS symptoms, diagnosis, prevention, and treatment. There is a lot of focus on prevention in order to curb prevalence rates. Furthermore, a prevention-focused intervention directly address the gender-based constraints that contribute to the worldwide HIV/AIDS epidemic, especially gender norms and practices that encourage high-risk sexual behavior for men. It is also important to address cultural beliefs that may contribute to HIV prevalence, including those that promote sex with virgins as a way to rid oneself of HIV/AIDS. It is important to begin early by engaging boys in small groups because socialization of gender norms and practices begins at birth. 3. HIV/AIDS education in school curriculumAs a third intervention, we might consider the introduction of materials on HIV/AIDS in school curricula. It is possible to include it in all subjects. This will not only educate girls and boys about HIV/AIDS (symptoms, diagnosis, prevention, and treatment), but also generate a community of understanding around the virus and syndrome. I find it interesting that linear regression can be considered a flexible model. In one sense linear regression is not considered a flexible model and as such, is more interpretable. This is traditional thought based on the availability of a large number of observations in the data set with a relatively small number of predictors. In the sense of chapter six, the linear regression model becomes flexible due to the number of observations in the data set being not much larger than the number of predictors. So now the linear regression model suffers from coefficient estimates with large variance and is at risk of over-fitting. In the case of p > n, we have multiple solutions fitting the least squares and must consider how to choose between them. For this high-dimensional case, we also fall short on assessing model fit with traditional measures such as RSS, p-values, and R^2. In spite of all this, the linear model continues to be a simple, interpretable model and worth this study. In the end, we know not the true form of the relationship or even if there is a relationship. However, we can do our best to choose the appropriate method to answer the question. I wish I had these tools in my statistical belt 10 years ago :)

MLE means Maximum Likelihood Estimate. This is a method for estimating the value of a parameter that has the highest probability of being correct. The general idea is that you look at the product of the distribution function (pdf) at each data point, and find the value of the parameter that maximizes this expression. This expression is called the likelihood function. Most often, it is much easier to compute the derivative of the log of the likelihood function. While reading about Ridge Regression, I got to wondering why it's called Ridge Regression. I was not satisfied by my web search. So, I would appreciate if someone would like to share. What I did learn is the method is also known as Tikhonov regularization. It is used to address the problem of multicollinearity, such as may be the case when time and world population may be two predictors in a model of global warming. Where time and population increase at a similar rate. Multicollinearity is quantified by the variance inflation factor or VIF, which we can find in the output of statistical software programs. When this is the case and we wish to keep both predictors in the model for valid reasons, we can use Ridge Regression to address the issues caused by multicollinearity. Such issues include changing coefficient estimates and p-values when a collinear predictor is added to the model. This makes interpretation very tricky. These issues are caused by the large variance of our coefficient estimates due to the determinant of our XtransposeX matrix being close to zero. Ridge Regression adds on a factor which penalizes large parameter values. This is the same as adding a factor to our XtransposeX matrix and results in a determinant far from zero. This in turn reduces the variance of our parameter estimates at the cost of now they are no longer unbiased estimates of the true value. Perhaps the determinant is the ridge?Ref: http://tamino.wordpress.com/2011/02/12/ridge-regression/

Acceleration is any change in velocity relative to the straight line things go in it not affected by other forces. So if you are in that same car, and you turn to the left that's an acceleration too, and you feel a force to the right. The same thing is happening in orbit in space - you would travel in a straight line, but gravity causes your course to bend downward toward the earth. So there is a force you feel away from the earth.In a stable orbit (one that stays the same distance from earth) the outward force you feel from acceleration toward the earth is exactly balanced by the force of gravity pulling you toward the earth. (Neat fact here - one key part Einstein's theories of relativity is this fact - that there is no actual difference between gravity and acceleration). So, since the force from acceleration is exactly the same as the force of gravity, you feel no gravity.Again, by relativity, you are truly experiencing microgravity. it's just that if you stopped in orbit, there would be no force to counteract gravity and you would start getting closer to the earth -- in this case, not a good outcome.In truth, any time you are in free fall, your downward acceleration exactly matches the acceleration from gravity (because that's what free fall is) and you will, as a result, be weightless. In a plane, you can be in free fall for a few seconds. In orbit, because we are moving sideways while we fall, we can (with care) set things up so that we fall at the same rate as the earth's surface falls away from the straight line we'd take without gravity. Since our falling matches the curvature of the earth, we stay in orbit.But fundamentally, it is the fact that we are in free fall that causes the balance of forces that is weightlessness (or more precisely, microgravity)

The major physiological adaptation allowing divers to endure the lack of oxygen during apnea is the diving response.Our body system has inputs that interact with major central nervous system centers to activate when needed. The inputs are facial cold receptors, baroreceptors, carotid chemoreceptors, atrial receptors and pulmonary stretch receptors. These inputs all project to the nucleus tractus solitarius (NTS) and then continue on to one of three central nervous system centers: the respiratory center, the cardiac parasympathetic center, or the vasomotor center. In response to apnea the above receptors interact in the NTS and project to either inhibit or excite their respective control center and thus produce the cardiovascular responses associated with the diving response. Reliance on the biomedical model undermines the introduction of social interventions by fostering the assumption that non-medical interventions are inherently inferior and less effective than medical solutions.  Non-medical interventions to epidemics like HIV/AIDS, however, can not only be effective, but have the potential, in a way that medical interventions do not, of creating long-term structural change that may prevent the spread of HIV/AIDS as well as numerous other diseases.  Beyond disease prevention, the lasting implications of social interventions for human rights and quality of life are far reaching.  For example, outreach and awareness campaigns aimed at eliminating myths and reducing the stigma of HIV/AIDS, and promoting (and providing) free, confidential testing, could reduce the incidence and fatality of the disease by making more people aware of their status and how to either stay negative or live healthily with positive diagnoses.  Beyond this, it could lead to better treatment of people living with HIV/AIDS and fewer negative consequences associated with a positive diagnosis.  If receiving a positive diagnosis had fewer social consequences, people would be much more likely to be willing to receive testing and learn about how to take care of their health, whether positive or negative.It is clear from the readings, however, that education alone is insufficient to prevent the spread of HIV/AIDS.  Many women, for example, know the facts about the disease and how it is spread, and may even know they are at high risk of contracting HIV, but do not have the bargaining power to negotiate safe sexual encounters, or the social power to explore options for alternative ways of defining womanhood. Marital norms that give men sexual license while prohibiting women from advocating for their own needs, and expectations that women must bear children, make it difficult for women and girls the world over to negotiate for safe sex within a marriage, which can place her, and any potential children, at high risk for contracting HIV/AIDS. This suggests that structural interventions aimed at normalizing discussions of sex, sexuality and condom use within relationships - for both men and women - could help empower women to have a voice in their relationships, and empower both men and women to engage in healthier ways of relating.  This could happen through comprehensive sex education, radio and TV shows that normalize the subject matter and make it accessible,

Teen boys can also work together to understand HIV prevention and how to be responsible. Such programmes can be adapted by age group, done in schools and through non formal education.2) Awareness programmes can take many forms in terms of media campaigns, rallies, ribbon campaigns, etc. World AIDS Day held on 1st December is an example where events are held around the world each year. There will be some bias in the estimate of the MSE if you are both tuning the model *and* estimating the MSE at the same time.Double CV is often used when you need to tune *and* estimate the model. Essentially you have an outer CV loop, say a $k$-fold with $k = 5$, and then within each fold you do an entire CV (another $k$-fold for example or a bootstrap CV). The inner fold is to choose the values of the parameters you want to tune (number of components etc) and then you fit the tuned model and use it to predict for the fold left out in the outer loop. Repeat for all folds in the outer loop.That said, it is my understanding that the bias in tuning *and* estimating the error at the same time is not that large in many cases. Whether that bias is larger or smaller than the bias introduced by fitting CV models to even smaller subsets of the training data is something I can't answer.

Why do we talk about the feeling of floating in a lecture on microgravity? Because floating (in space) ***is*** microgravity. If we ignore the sun and stop all motion, there is only one place in the earth-moon system where gravitational pull is zero -- at point near the moon where where the pull of the smaller moon is equal and opposite to the pull of the earth. But in practice, there are many other situations in space where we feel the effects of microgravity.This is because gravity and acceleration are indistinguishable from one another, so acceleration can counter the gravity of a body in space in just the same way gravity does. Free fall is accelerating at a rate that counterbalances gravity, and if you are free-falling in  plane with no windows you will be floating within the plane.*Floating is free-fall, and free-fall is zero gravity.*The special thing about a stable orbit is simply that you can be in free fall indefinitely.

I think I may see where your confusion lies, though.CV is a method for estimating how much error we'll get if we first train a certain model (e.g. forward stepwise with 5 steps) on a training set and then make predictions on new test data.To get a good estimate, we train on 9/10 of the training data (the \training fold\") and make predictions for 1/10 of the training data (the \"test fold\" or \"validation fold\"), and then repeat that ten times and average the results.  The test folds come from the training data but they are *playing the role* of test data in our CV procedure.We don't want to use the test folds for model selection inside of CV because then we'd get a biased estimate of how good the model is.  But now say we are done with CV, and we have chosen the model size.  At that point, we should go back to thinking of all our data as training data.  Naturally, then we want to use as much training data as possible in training the final model."

You may have noticed that some functions in R do different things depending on the class of argument you pass.  For example, if x is a numeric vector plot(x) does something different from what it does if x is a lm fit. This works because plot is what's called a \generic\" function with multiple \"methods\" (think of these as different behaviors it can have) for different data types.  There are two ways that you can write generic functions in R.  One is by using \"S3 methods\" and the other is by using \"S4 methods.\"  Unless you plan to write your own R package, the differences aren't really important.  What matters to an end user is that if you see \"S3 method\" in the documentation of a function, then there is a generic function that calls that function for particular types of data.  For example, plot.lm is the S3 method that the generic function plot calls in order to show the diagnostic plots for an lm object.Hope that helps."

Because additional trees are fitted to the *residuals* of the current fit. When the first tree is grown it is trying to fit the response as the response values are copied to the residuals vector. Then, a simple tree is fitted and a shrunken version of the fitted values is taken as the contribution of that tree to the fit. The residuals are reduced by the same amount, ready for the next tree.When the second tree is grown, because each tree is fitted to the *residuals* (**not** the observed values of the response), the fit is improved some more and with it the bias is reduced a little bit; the two trees more closely follow the data than the first tree alone.As you keep adding trees, those trees explain aspects of the data not well fitted by the set of previously fitted trees. If you were to keep on fitting, eventually you'd explain all the variance in the data: the residuals would be reduced to zero, and hence there'd be *no* bias [but high variance at that point]. Achieving this takes a long time with boosted trees because of the shrinkage applied to the fitted values of each tree; hence boosted trees learn slowly.Contrast this with randomForests; there we have the same ensemble of trees, but each tree is fitted to the same response vector of data/observations. The stochasticity introduced via bagging and the random selection of `mtry` parameters for each split-selection reduces models that can be averaged over, to reduce variance.I can't quite think of a good way to explain what is happening to the bias in a randomForest; you are fitting a (potentially) low bias, high variance tree to a bootstrap sample of the data because you grow each tree large, but as you only consider random subsets of the available variables to form each split in those trees, they could still be biased. There are 4 reasons to always have a test data set (assuming you have a large data set with more than 1 MM observations):1. You may be using CV the wrong way (and not know it). As explained in lecture, if you have 1,000 variables and pre-screen them using bi-variate correlations between each x and y, then your CV estimate of test set error may be overly optimistic. 2. The right way to use CV would be to include variable pre-screening at each fold. However, if you have a large data set, doing CV the right way might be computationally intensive. For example, if you do 10-fold CV with 1 MM observations, you're pre-screening the variables 10 times where **each** iteration would use 900,000 observations to pre-screen 1,000 variables. If you had a 70% training/30% test splilt, you would prescreen the variables once on 700,000 training observations.3. If you use CV to estimate tuning parameters **and** use CV to estimate test set error, your CV test set error may be overly optimistic. I often use CV to choose tuning parameters, but use a test set to estimate test set error.4. Comparing CV test set errors between two models (e.g., lasso vs. trees) may be problematic unless you correctly set the seed values. By default, 10-fold CV randomly assigns an observation to one fold. If you run 10-fold CV repeatedly, an observation might end up in different folds. For example, you run cv.glmnet(), observation 1 might be in fold 9. If you run cv.tree() observation 1 might be in fold 10. The CV test set errors are not comparable because the compositions of the folds are different! You can avoid this (I think) by setting the same seed value right before running each cv function.

I'm not sure why you think the standard errors for the coefficients are assumption-free?  They are based on an assumption of (at least approximate by an appeal to the CLT in large samples) normality.  The assumptions for the standard errors of the $hat{Y}$s is the same.  (EDIT: On a purely practical note, whenever you bother to find the standard error of a statistic, you probably should be assuming the sampling distribution of the statistic is approximately normal because otherwise the standard error is not a terribly useful summary of the shape of the distribution and hence not a good measure of the uncertainty in the statistic.)Remember that in linear regression we are assuming that $hat{Y}=hat{f}(X)$ is a linear (in the parameters) function of $X$ (i.e., it is an estimate of $E[Y|X]$ under an assumption about the functional form: $E[Y|X]=f(X)$).  Once we have a set of data $(X_i,Y_i)$, we can estimate the parameters and hence the functional form $hat{f}(X)=hat{Y}$ as a function of $X$. Then, we can estimate the mean value of the response $Y$ on a new explanatory value $X_{new}$ as $hat{Y}_{new}=hat{f}(X_{new})$, based on the observed data $(X_i,Y_i)$.  Also based on the same observed data, we can estimate the standard error of $hat{Y}_{new}$ using the formula you gave in your first post above (which is based on the assumption of normality).  Alternately, we can estimate the standard error of $hat{Y}(X_{new})$ by taking lots (say $B$) of bootstrap samples of the observed data $(X_i,Y_i)$, fitting the model to each bootstrap sample, calculating $hat{Y}_{new,j}=hat{f}_j(X_{new})$ for $j=1cdots B$, and then finding the standard deviation of $hat{Y}_{new,j}$ for $j=1cdots B$.  Note however that if the sampling distribution of $hat{Y}_{new}$ is not close to being normal (e.g., if the histogram of $hat{Y}_{new,j}$ is not well approximated by a normal distribution) , the standard error of $hat{Y}_{new}$ will not be useful as a summary of uncertainty (e.g., the CIs calculated from it will not have the nominal coverage).  In that case, it would be better to form a CI on $hat{Y}_{new}$ using quantiles of the sampling distribution.  On the other hand, if the sampling distribution is close to being normal, then (I suspect) the bootstrap standard errors and the calculated standard errors should be close to the same.  Similar statements to the above apply to the standard errors and CIs for the coefficients as well. The result of 5.5.R.1 does not require any claim about orderings.First, attach to each of the points in the data set a unique label and think of them as uniquely colored balls in a box. Then, to obtain one bootstrap sample of size n, we independently sample n times from the box with replacement. Since the probability of not selecting one particular ball is (n-1)/n, the result follows as a consequence of n independent trials. On the other hand, you may be concerned as to why we allow two sets, 1,2,3 and 2,1,3 to be 2 different bootstrap samples. In fact, the bootstrap procedure treats each of the B samples differently and equally. The occurrence of (1,2,3) and (2,1,3) among the set of samples simply indicates that the histogram/distribution of the points 1, 2 and 3 are rather uniform resulting in many identically looking samples. Intuitively, if you are monitoring pairs of consecutive coin flips, it wouldn't be surprising to see many Head-Head sequences.Hope this helps(:

Ideally, given a sample size n, we would like to evaluate estimates based on all n observations. However, in cross validation, we are leaving some part of the sample out in every iteration. As a result, the effective sample size shrinks. Hi there, changing the order of columns will not affect the predictive power of the model. Theoretically speaking, orthogonalization is done via the gram schmidt procedure. That is, we use the first column as a reference and project the second column onto it to create an orthogonal vector. Then we use the third to project on the space span by the first and the second, and so on. Therefore, if you change the column of the design matrix it will certainly change the output of your orthogonalization. However, the seemingly different output is merely a rotation of the output you would have gotten if you have used the original orientation. Don't take my word for it. It is easy to see using say PCA for example. Note that if you change the columns of your design matrix, the loadings associated will change. However, the proportion of variation explained will remain the same.Hope this helps~

And, to answer the other implied question, in case you were wondering...*Why did you use `data=whatever` before and don't need it now?*For this question, your `x` and `y` variables exist \out in the open\", all by themselves. When you type \"x\", for example, R knows exactly which vector you're talking about.This is rare case!In most examples (and in real life, usually) the parameters used in your formula are actually columns (vectors) in a **data frame**. Just specifying the column name alone isn't enough for R to know what you're talking about--you have to *also* tell it the data frame to look in.So let's say `x` and `y` *were* in a data frame called, for example, `foo`. You could **not** do this:        fit <- lm(y ~ x)...because R wouldn't have a variable called \"y\" or \"x\". Or, even worse, it would have an x and y variable left over from some previous session that was still sitting around, and it would use that instead of the data you really intended!But you **could** do this:        fit <- lm( foo$y ~ foo$x )...because R *does* have a variable called \"foo\", which contains the \"x\" and \"y\" vectors.And, as a sort of shortcut, you can also do this:        fit <- lm( y ~ x, data=foo)That tells R, \"When I say `x` and `y`, I really mean the x and y that live inside of `foo`.\""

To answer question 1,Let \A\" be the original set of data and \"B\" to be a bootstrapped sample from A. Naturally B is a subset of A and from 36/51 in the lecture notes on trees, B has on average 2/3 of the values in A. Thus, we can use the other 1/3 to do validating.Now one might be quick to jump in and say that this is 3-fold cross-validation but this is not exactly. In k-fold cross validation, we slice the original sample up into k different parts and then do the validating by building the model on all except one part. In OOB however, notice that although B is approximately 2/3 of A, the composition is not deterministic. Also, in k-fold cross validation, we need only to perform k computation and average them. On the other hand, OOB does it as many times as the number of Bootstrap samples required.All in all, OOB is some kind of cross validation though we cannot directly pin point the number of folds it is doing. Since it is naturally to add an additional prediction step for the other 1/3 of the sample that is not included in the bootstrapped sample, it is only computationally wise to just compute it internally. Rest assure, it is definitely an unbiased estimate of the errors as expectation is linear and thus averaging it over B estimates don't matter versus K estimates. The only thing that will differ could be the estimated variance of the error rate since variance generally decreases as the number of samples increase (e.g. for variance of mean is (sigma^2)/n). Then again, its not straightforward to compute the variance of the error rates in OOB since the samples are correlated. (e.g. var(x+y) = var(x) + var(y) + *2cov(x,y)*)Hope this helps ~"

Sure.  No problem.  As to the CLT and the irreducible errors, I guess I was making a subtle distinction in a not very clear way.  Expecting the irreducible errors to be typically be nearly normal by an appeal to the CLT as stated in the wikipedia article is sort of a philosophical choice...but it should be checked to see if they really are in any given situation.  And if they aren't, gathering more data probably won't make them that way.  The data generating mechanism either has noise that is a sum of independent random jolts or it doesn't.  On the other hand, gathering more data will tend to make the sampling distribution of the parameters more normal by the CLT because they are estimated as sums of the observed responses weighted by combinations of the observed explanatory variables.  So as long as the irreducible errors aren't from some pathological distribution that the CLT doesn't apply to, we can expect the betas to be distributed normally if we gather enough data.

not sure about the problem at hand, but the scalar 36.04 should be $sqrt{n - 1}$.  Consider the followingcalculate the eigenvalues of the covariance matrix for $x$.  i.e.,     eig.val.cov <- eigen(cov(x))$valuesNext, calc the singular values of $x$    svd.d <- svd(x)$d; If you square the singular values of $x$ and divide by $n - 1$ where $n$ is the number of records in $x$, you end up with the eigenvalue for the covariance matrix.  You will see that they agree.  This is no accident and is due to the way the singular values decompsition is calculated.  WLOG suppose that each column of $X$ has 0 mean and unit variance, then we compute the covariance matrix as $frac{1}{n-1} X^TX$.  Basically (not 100% correct) the SVD computes the eigenvectors and eigenvalues for $XX^T$ and $X^TX$.  Now if $X$ is $m$ by $n$, then the first $n$ eigenvalues of $XX^T$ will coincide with the eigenvalues of $X^TX$ and the remaining $m-n$ eigenvalues of $XX^T$  will be 0.  The square root of the eigenvalues are the singular values of $X$.
