wrt part 2, missing data, there are several options. Which one you use depends on your objectives, the data and any patterns in the missing data. The simplest choice is to deleted any cases with missing values, see complete.cases in R. This is fine so long as you have sufficient data and there is no pattern in the missing cases, there is of course a downside, you've lost the information in the deleted cases and also you've built a model that cannot handle missing data in the test set. Alternatively you can fill the missing data in (called imputation) with an appropriate value, say mean or median. If you do so, you should create an additional predictor that marks which values were imputed, do this for each predictor seperately. Then you can build your model using the new improved set of predictors (no missing values). If the added predictors are significant, it tells you there may be a pattern in the missing values that can be useful in prediction. There are more complicated methods including multiple imputation (see google). Alternatively (again) some methods can handle missing values natively (for instance random forests). Two references are Little and Rubin - Data Analysis with missing data, though I generally prefer Enders - Applied Missing Data Analysis.Unfortunately which is best depends on your objective and the data. If you don't care about missing values in the test (or real world usage) and you have sufficient data you can delete the cases, else you need to develop an imputation scheme and which is best is data dependent. Which ever you use I recommend adding the extra predictors, it is not uncommon to find patterns in missing bits.

Then given these, perhaps you can combine them in some way that would be better than just selecting the optimal for the training set overall.For example, if you had a way to compute variable importance like the random forest does, you could take the average (CV) importance for each of the variables/genes through CV, then take the top ones (however many you want to use) to form your optimal set. In other words, the top ones would be those genes that hopefully keep showing up as important when predicting the validation set (the $1/K$th fraction from CV). \i.i.d.\" means \"independent and identically distributed\". Normal bootstrapping tacitly assumes that there is no connection between subsequent data points, i.e. that they are independent. This makes sense for a lot of kinds of data: if you sample 100 voters, it doesn't matter whether John Smith is data point #2 or #99 - his voting behavior is determined by other things (political stance, campagin ads, whatever). A lot of statistical methods require that this is true for the data, so that you can in effect look at a single data point without considering which ones come before/after it.Some kinds of data, however, are NOT independent. If you take the weather of 100 consecutive days, the user ratings of 10 consecutive versions of a product, or other data that develops over time, it matters a great deal what came before a given data point: we all know that today's weather depends a lot on yesterday's weather, and so the weather of day #2 depends a lot on the weather of day #1. Product updates (and thus user satisfaction) depend a lot on user satisfaction with the previous version. By (wrongly) assuming that these data are independent, we lose a lot of the information that determines/predicts a data point.(Block bootstrapping addresses this by sampling not individual data points, but consecutive blocks of data points, so that at least the connections between the points in each block are preserved.)"

I loved reading the book “From Outrage to Courage.” Even from the very subtitle, “The Unjust and Unhealthy Situation of Women in Poorer Countries and What THEY Are Doing About It,” Professor Murray seems to turn traditional power dynamics on their head. We are not posed as students learning only how to help the atrocious Human Rights inequalities in the world, but learning how those disenfranchised women are helping themselves gain power, in this global human rights movement, as part of the third wave of feminism discussed in the last chapter. “They,” women of the world, are taking their power and voice. “They” are not asking other authorities to give them power, but demanding it, in her statement. I add the emphasis to the word “they” because I see the very use of “they” versus “we” gives the power, control and agency not to “us”  students, other members of society, or men, to save women, but back to the women themselves to help run their lives. Helping those in need is a beautiful thing, but to create something local, sustainable, allowing autonomy is even more important. Because of this **demand**, hence students are willing to give up college to enter NBA. To the promising young basketball player who wants to build his basketball career, the opportunity cost of going to college and not playing in NBA is significantly higher than the opportunity cost of dropping out and playing in the NBA. In order to make a decision that is best aligned to his/her ambitions and has the lowest opportunity cost, hence it is understandable why dropout occurs. **No Restriction or Increase the Limit? **The restriction should be dropped altogether, because the opportunity cost of going to college and subsequently dropping out is more substantial than the opportunity cost of not going to college altogether and entering the NBA right after high school. For the individual himself/herself, college is not as ideal a training ground for basketball specific skills as compared to the NBA. Given that a NBA career places an extremely high premium on basketball skills (e.g. dribbling, passing, etc.) rather than skills and knowledge picked up from college classes, the one year in college before the individual drops out has a high opportunity cost (that is, not being able to focus 100% on playing basketball as he would have in NBA).If the individual can play basketball right after high school in NBA, the opportunity cost is a college education. However, this is a lower opportunity cost than one year of college (with less rigorous basketball-training), because the student desires to pursue a career in NBA. Entering NBA right after high school means no time lost from spending one year in college, hence lower opportunity cost.

Assume that the NBA’s only purpose is to maximize revenue and profits, and that revenue and profits are maximized when games are played by the best available basketball players.  In the absence of any rule, available players will make decisions about the value of playing basketball and the value of going to college, which is the opportunity cost of choosing professional basketball.  With a rule that potential players must sit out one year after high school, the value to a player of playing in the NBA for that year is zero, and the value of attending college for one year is no longer the opportunity cost of playing in the NBA in that year, which is not an alternative. If the value of attending college for one year is greater than the value of some alternative activity, a player will attend college. However, the players for whom the value of a basketball career is much more valuable than a career whose vlaue is enhanced by attending college will leave college after one year.  Hence, the only effect of the rule is likely to be that the NBA reduces the availability of the best players by one year. With a rule that potential players must sit out until they have graduated from college, available players must make a decision between the value of going to college and then playing in the NBA and the value of pursuing some alternative career, the new opportunity cost of playing in the NBA.  Under that rule, players unable to graduate from college do not have the possibility of playing in the NBA, and assuming the absence of these players reduces the NBA revenue, the rule simply harms the NBA’s interests, and the interests of potential players.  For players able to graduate from college, and for whom a career being paid to play basketball is much more valuable than a career whose value is enhanced by attending college, the rule simply reduces the value of their basketball career by four or perhaps more years.  For the NBA, the absence of those players while they are attending college probably reduces NBA revenue and does so to a much larger extent than the one year rule, and would appear to be in the NBA’s interests only if 4 plus years of college basketball experience enhances a player’s ability during a shortened NBA career, or allows the NBA better to select players by evaluating them based on their college careers.

If the price is fixed, the landlord has no incentive to improve his apartment complex to make it more attractive and earn a higher price, so instead he/she may allow it to deteriorate, leaving the renters living in poor conditions. Hi Brad,This is a great question. It's true that the models we consider in this class are very simple, but you would be surprised at how far we can go with these simple models. The PPC illustrates the trade-offs that agents make between any two goods that are produced using the same fixed set of available resources. Even if we consider just two goods, we can already illustrate the principle of increasing opportunity costs, which is a principle that also applies to an economy with more than two goods. In practice, economists don't draw PPCs for every possible combination of two goods. Instead, they use mathematical tools to solve optimization problems whose solution will be the optimal bundle of goods that agents should consume. I think the resolution is that consumers have a wide variety of options of products on which to spend their money.For example, say I'm a consumer who has 10 dollars to spend.There is a product X that costs 4 dollars / unit has a marginal benefit of 5 dollars for 1 unit purchased and a marginal benefit of 3 dollars for 2 units purchased.If, as a consumer with a 10 dollar budget, product X is the only product available for me to purchase in the market, I will maximize my utility (total marginal benefit) by purchasing two of product X for a total utility of 8 dollars.However, let's introduce a product Y that costs 4 dollars / unit and has a marginal benefit of 4 dollars for 1 unit purchased and a marginal benefit of 2 dollars for 2 units purchased.Now, as a consumer, I can maximize my utility (total marginal benefit) by purchasing 1 unit of product X and 1 unit of product Y for a total utility of 9 dollars.If either product X or product Y exists in isolation, my maximum utility is achieved by purchasing two units of the product. However, if both of these products exist together in the market -- a good model of the real world -- then I will purchase one of each.In general, a purchase can be thought of as a transaction of value, and consumers will optimize utility (total marginal benefit) among many product options by only making positive or break even value transactions.For example, let product Z cost 4.50 dollars / unit and have a marginal benefit of 5 dollars for 1 unit purchased and 3 dollars for 2 units purchased.Purchasing 1 unit of product Z is a value transaction of - 4.50 dollars of monetary value and + 5 dollars of marginal benefit value for a total value of + 0.50 dollars. It is in a consumer's best interest to make this positive value transaction.However, purchasing 2 units of product Z is a value transaction of - 9 dollars of monetary value and + 8 dollars of marginal benefit value for a total value of - 1 dollars. A consumer will avoid this negative value transaction in a market with many options in favor of other value transactions that are positive or break even in total value payoff.

Shifts in supply occur when something besides a change in price changes the quantity of a good that people are willing to sell.Although it may seem like that as the price increases, you have more \demand\", in reality, the demand has not shifted at all. This seems a bit counterintuitive. Let me repeat. The demand has not increased for bicycles nor has it increased. The quantity supplied however, changes in response to changes in price.i.e. as the price increases, the quantity supplied increases. The demand does not change. As the price decreases, the quantity supplied decreases.Another way of looking at it is the equilibrium supply and demand model. As we go up along the demand curve as the price increases, so too does our supply increase. As we go down along the demand curve as the price decreases, so too does supply respond in turn. What happens if we change the demand or change the supply. Well, if we translate our demand curve to the right, then the equilibrium price will increase which results in a net increase for the price of the bicycles. If the amount of bicycles supplied decreases, the supply curve is translated to the left. That in turn raises the equilibrium price which also in turn raises the price. It's very subtle, but it has a lot of implications. Price increase and quantity supplied means movement along the demand curve. Alternatively, you can think about if price decreases, then the amount supplied decreases. Market equilibrium, however will gravitate towards when the amount demanded equals the amount supplied. Demand increases shifts the equilibrium price up (think translation of the demand curve), and if supply is kept the same, raises prices. If the supply of bicycles increases (think again translation of the supply curve), and the demand is kept constant, the equilibrium price decreases, and price decreases. I feel as if Professor Taylor could have stressed this fact in the preceding video before the quiz; however, the video with market equilibrium after the quiz was illuminating and really brought all these concepts together."

But here are my responses to the questions above:Q:  Is the market for housing in San Francisco Pareto efficient?  What about deadweight loss?  A:  The current housing market in San Francisco is not Pareto efficient.  One condition that must be met if a market is to be Pareto efficient is this:  the marginal benefit, or demand curve, must intersect the marginal cost, or supply curve, at a single point. This is lost surplus for the suppliers as the buyers are benefitted. One possible alternative may be to use legislative oversight to approve changes in regulatory policy as a foil to regulatory capture and industry influence. The thing is, \education\" isn't one single thing. It can be split up into \"elementary education,\" \"secondary education,\" and \"college education.\" And in fact, even \"college education\" can be split into the separate *products*, if you can call it that, of \"public college education,\" \"Ivy League education,\" etc. With that in mind, let's see which of these are public goods.First off, elementary and secondary education are public goods. They are state-funded, and barring the cases of the severely understaffed schools in impoverished areas, they are non-rival and non-excludable (although the students do have the option to drop out after a certain point).As for college education, this is where it gets tricky. A college education is definitely excludable when the product being sold is \"college education at Harvard,\" but not so much when it is \"college education at your local community college.\" It is non-rival if the product is \"college education from online classes,\" but it is rival if the product is \"college education at ________ exclusive university\" (although you could argue that relative to the people already in the university, it is non-rival because attending lectures is free).One unifying factor, though, is that education causes positive externalities. An informed populace has higher wealth, satisfaction, and quality of life. Even those who do not have a higher education benefit from economic increases caused by those who do. The government is therefore subsidizing college education for many incoming college students. Of course, this comes with downsides too: because more students are being subsidized, colleges raise tuition costs, contributing to the rampant problem of student debt. This is, in fact, a negative externality of subsidies given to only certain students. The ones who aren't subsidized have to face a higher cost."

Now the government introduces the wage cap. This causes a movement along the labour supply curve - the price of labour has been set, so the quantity supplied will drop accordingly. Firms demand more labour than is available, so there is a deficit of labour, but the cap prevents them from raising wages in response. As the quantity of labour is reduced, the quantity of goods produced is reduced. This reduces the marginal cost of production (diminishing returns on labour mean it's more efficient to produce smaller amounts).At this lower quantity of production, demand is higher than supply, so the price is higher than the marginal cost of producing the goods. This leads to a deadweight loss in the market, but also a profit for the firms. So, lower quantity, higher price, lower marginal costs. The paper written by the two economists argues the point of how the Department of Justice erred far better than I could.  From what I gather, the antitrust regulations of the Sherman Act and other legislation define price fixing in a necessarily narrow and limited fashion.  If it did not, conceivably any action by a group of firms could be construed as price fixing.  For example, if a shortage of a given material critical to production in a given industry drove all firms in that industry to raise their prices, this could be called \price fixing\" in that the all firms seemingly \"conspired\" to raise their prices.Fortunately, our country's antitrust legislation does not leave this loophole open.  Price fixing is defined specifically as \"horizontal\" collusion between firms in an industry to set the price at a level that would not otherwise be in the independent firms' interests.  We can think of the game theory example here for a duopoly, where if each firm were to act independently of the other, both would elect to \"cheat\" or lower their prices in order to sell more product.  Independent of each other, this is how they would behave, for it is in the best interest of each firm to do so.  Collusion and price-fixing occurs when both firms agree to set the price higher and sell less, separate from the independent benefit each would see from selling more at a lower price.As the amici curiae paper argues, Apple's actions do not fall into this narrow definition, and thus cannot be rightly considered \"price fixing.\"  This was not \"horizontal\" collusion - Apple did not conspire with Amazon and agree to raise prices.  It is unlikely that Amazon would have even entered into such an agreement, since they already owned the majority of the market share and would have seen Apple only as a potential competitor that they would like to keep out of the market if they could.  Instead, Apple had to find a roundabout way to gain entry into the market at all - going directly to the publishers, who were already unhappy with the losses in their profits due to the rise of ebooks and Amazon's ability to undercut competitive prices. In theory, I believe education should be a public good, but in our current school systems it is not. There is a massive quality gap in education that is a result of public versus private funding, quality of the school district, presence of charter schools, and institutional practices. Because the quality of education is not the same across the nation, it cannot be deemed a public good in the same way that national defense can. Education is rivalrous and excludable. It is excludable because certain social injustices prevent certain types of students from accessing education in the same ways that other students are able to. For example, individuals coming from various socio-economic statuses may have varying resources to buy school supplies, receive help on homework, receive proper nutrition for development, etc. As compared to national defense where anyone receives protection regardless of race, class, or gender, education does not provide the same blanket coverage. Additionally, education is rivalrous. I would consider education to be a limited resource, especially higher education such as college. There are a limited number of spots for attendance and a limited number of scholarships to enable students to attend college. For this reason, education is rivalrous because one student's access prevents another student from accessing it. In a perfect world, education would be a public good provided with equal quality to all people but that is not the current state of affairs in the United States education system.

I'm going to disagree with many of the other posts here and argue that while traditional elementary education may be *delivered* like a public good in countries like the US, it is fundamentally no different from private postsecondary education (not a public good).**Not non-rival:** A single teacher can only teach a finite number of students, and the quality of education is generally accepted as higher in smaller classes. Adding another child to a classroom either displaces another child or decreases the quality of education for the rest of the class.**Not non-excludable:** Barring someone access to education is as simple as restricting their physical access to a school. Looking at global access to education issues (particularily among girls and young women) makes this painfully clear.Given that even traditional elementary level education can be shown to be neither non-rival nor non-excludable, I  would contend that it is not a public good, at any level (unfortunately). However, advances in technology (infinite duplicability and access to information via the internet, and MOOCs like this one) are in the process of changing that.However, I would agree that education has significant positive externalities, in particular at the lowest levels (elementary, etc). The benefits of a literate population, for example, are far greater than the sum of private benefits to literate individuals. In my view it's these major positive externalities that justify delivering elementary education publicly (ie completely subsidized).

Is GDP a fair and accurate representation of national health? That depends on what is meant by \national health.\" By national health do we mean we are happier, have less problems such as sudden infant deaths, chronic diseases, and less crime? If this is what is meant by national health, then GDP is a poor measure.Even when we talk about economic health, GDP is found wanting. GDP is suppose to be the value of all final goods and services produced within a country's borders over some period of time, but it does not adjust for the value of economic resources that have been destroyed, not just depleted. The Great Plains have a season in which tornadoes strike and destroy homes and other structures, not to mention injury to people and loss of human life. The same with hurricane season on the East and Gulf Coasts. After such catastrophes, people rebuild and this rebuilding is counted toward GDP, but the value of the economic resources that were destroyed or made unusable is not factored into this measure of the \"health of the economy.\"Realizing that any measure of how a country is doing will have its flaws, I would suggest that besides GDP  we include a measure of economic losses for the period to offset the value lost in such things as catastrophes. The measure might also include some human factors such as a measure of income inequality knowing that the economy cannot remain robust over the long term if a great proportion of the population is not receiving a portion of the gains from a growing economy. Thus some \"national progress index\" would supplement GDP with a measure of economic losses due to accidents, natural disasters and other catastrophes. Property insurance claims might be used as one estimate for such losses. Another would be an estimate of the economic value that could have been created had there been less income inequality. Thus something like the Gini index may be employed, but selecting a \"desirable\" level to represent a preferable income distribution to be achieved is open to controversy and is unlikely to gain universal agreement.Americans have one of the highest per capita income levels in the world, but in one survey they also were said to be among the angriest people in the world. This is a very complex and multifaceted dynamic which I do not think can be explained only in terms of supply and demand for tech labor. Additionally, the roe of market finance and the growth of \tech bubbles\" has also been significant.  But, the article does make an interesting observation concerning how a high demand for tech labor may have limited the industry's growth to a degree, at least within Silicon Valley.Within the context of the supply-demand framework, a high demand for tech labor equates to an inadequate supply, or a shortage.  This will result in higher prices - higher wages - for the shorted labor.  One would expect, as the article argues, that the result of these high wages would be an influx of workers into the tech industry within Silicon Valley.  This result stems from the substitution effect - individuals would be motivated to forego leisure in favor of work as a result of the higher wages.However, the real-world numbers do not accurately reflect this prediction.  The author proposes that this results from the high housing costs in and around Silicon Valley.  He notes that housing costs rose at a rate higher than tech industry wages, meaning that the REAL WAGES - the living wages - actually decreased for the Silicon Valley area.  This can almost be thought of as the income effect for labor in reverse - workers would actually have less real income. It is very interesting to see that there are such conflicting data with regard to the employment effects of the minimum wage.  The supply and demand model for competitive markets would typically predict that a minimum wage would ALWAYS reduce employment.  However, there are several exceptions that I can think of, where perhaps a minimum wage carefully implemented would not have an overall negative effect on employment, as the article suggests.As Professor Taylor discussed in the video, a steep demand curve for labor would mean that a minimum wage would have very little effect on employment.  There are any number of factors that could lead to such a demand curve.  As the article alludes to, continuing technological advancements leading to greater workplace efficiency and ultimately greater productivity could offset the increase to production costs that come with a higher minimum wage.  Thus demand would keep pace with a rising wage, since firms would still be trying to maximize profits under the competitive paradigm, just with greater productive capacity as a result of technological advances.Additionally, the effects of minimum wage on employment depend on the segment of the labor population.  The competitive model does not predict reduced employment in labor markets where the market equilibrium wage is already above the minimum wage.  This is the equivalent of a government floor below the equilibrium price, which has no effect on the market, at least according to the supply and demand paradigm.  Thus, a cleverly implemented minimum wage could target specifically those low-income, unskilled labor segments that most need it at a time when overall employment in industry sectors that operate above the minimum wage is on the rise.  This would lead to a situation where overall employment numbers could potentially not be affected.  Theoretically, any decrease in employment in the unskilled segment would be offset by a growth in employment in a different sector.This might account for why some studies show that minimum wage does not affect employment, whereas others do.  It all depends on the segment of the labor market being analyzed and also on the timing - what is going on in the economy as a whole?  Is it growing? The thing about GDP is that it measures a very specific thing. Specifically, it measures the total amount of production in a country. Realize that, because the real world isn't perfectly competitive, and because big markets tend towards oligopoly, there is often a surplus of products produced, creating deadweight loss while technically increasing the statistic of GDP. If we define GDP as Y = C + I + G + (X-M), then increased consumption could increase the statistic. Think of WWII. While the average person wasn't so well off, the statistic of GDP went sky high simply because of the high government spending on the war. GDP doesn't measure the theoretical maximum-efficiency scenario; by definition, the government will be less Pareto-efficient than the market in its purchases.Overall, the measure of quality of life can be determined with the Human Development Index (HDI). Some people propose the Gini coefficient (a measure of inequality), but realistically, a country can have high inequality and still be well-off. Even the poorest citizens of the US survive on more money than the rest of the world. Of course, the cost of living also factors into this. The HDI takes all of this into consideration, and as a result, the highest-scoring nations are the wealthy Scandanavian, Western European, and Australian countries.

If government expenditures increase, then there is less GDP available for the other three shares. The percentage of GDP available would decrease, shifting the supply curve to the left, raising the interest rates, causing consumption, investment, and net exports to decrease. The new equilibrium disables GDP from being spent in other areas than government expenditure.

An increase in government share of GPD will, by definition, lower the shares of consumption, investment, and net exports. It is technically possible to increase the absolute amounts of C, I, or X while C/Y, I/Y, and X/Y decrease. However, unnecessary expenditures by the government artificially increase the total GDP, making it more difficult for each of these sectors to increase their share of the GDP. In order to stimulate higher percentage shares in the other sectors, the government would have to cut back on spending to lower the percentage share of governmental spending, decreasing the crowding-out effect.

Both theories have merits. For many people, having a job is honorable in the sense that they are able to support themselves and others. My first instinct to explain why the long-term unemployed have such difficulties finding jobs is that employers hold biases against such people. This is because the long-term unemployed may be thought to be less valuable in the work force because they have been out of work for such a long time and therefore may require more training (more time, more effort, creating higher costs at the expense of the company). It may also be that those who have been unemployed for the longest amount of time are also the least skilled workers available and therefore the least qualified for jobs. However, the second theory is also valid because unemployment benefits are so generous. Perhaps ironically, those who have been the longest unemployed may also be the same people reaping the most benefits from the federal jobless benefits cheques and therefore have even less incentive to return to the workforce.

You idea of \tailing off\" is a good way how to explain by logic not only the demand curve, but the supply curve as well. If a business owner or manufacturer sees an opportunity to sell for a higher price, he is incentivised by the price increase to produce and sell as much as possible. But since the resources (employees, premises, etc. factors of production) is limited business owner / manufacturer by the price increase tries to optimise and get the most out of the resources it has. So every time when price increases driven by innovation / efficiency / economy of scale / creativity it figures out how to supply even more at the price. The curve \"tails off\" when the production resources is close to its end and it is impossible to produce even more units than before because of the production possibility curve."

Thus Americans appear to be more focused on satisfying their wants and desires in the present and have become less concerned about focusing on the future.Canada, on the other hand, has not consumed as much as Americans as a proportion of GDP and in fact consumption to GDP declined slightly in the 50 years period shown in the data. This allowed Canadians to save more and these savings allowed for a greater proportion of GDP to be devoted to investment. The less rapaciousness of Canadians and their willingness to devote more income to investment is reflected in trade surpluses and a general increase in net exports over this time. So over the last 50 years or so, the American consumers were devoted to satisfying their own appetites while Canadians decided to consume less as a proportion of GDP so they could save and invest more in an effort to satisfy the appetites of Americans and foreign consumers as reflected in the increasing trade surpluses.One other thing may be mentioned. I posted this in response to someone else's question, but I see a number of posts asking similar questions, so I posted here as a general aid...Here's how to calculate mean, standard deviation and IQR from a frequency table (referencing homework 1)I do all of this in Excel by the way...Calculate the **mean** using the frequency table given by multiplying each outcome value (11, 12, etc.) by the number of times it occurs (frequency value).  You will end up with six products representing total breaths for each of the six breath outcomes.  For example, the outcome of 11 breaths occurs 10 times.  That's a total breath count of 110 breaths for those 10 people.  Do the same for the other 5 outcome values and their associated frequencies.  Now, add up the six products to get total breaths.  Then, divide that total by 60 to get the average breath count per person. That is your mean.To get the **standard deviation**, calculate the difference between a given breath outcome and your calculated mean (for example: 11 – calculated mean).  Now, square that difference and multiply it by the frequency for that outcome.  The general formula for any given outcome (i) for this first part is: ((outcome(i) – calculated mean)^2) * frequency(i).  In our example: ((11 – calculated mean) ^2) * 10.  That provides the total squared deviations for a single outcome.  Do the same for the other 5 outcome values using your calculated mean and the associated frequency for each outcome.  Now, add up those six total squared deviations to get the grand total squared deviation (GTSD).  Divide that number by n-1 (60-1).  Now, take the square root to get the standard deviation.  So the standard deviation = sqrt(GTSD/(n-1)).The **median** will be the average of two data points in the middle since n is even (60 data points).  So, the median will be the average of points 30 and 31.  What values are at points 30 and 31?  To calculate the IQR, you need the 25th and 75th percentiles. What values are at points 15 & 16?  The **75th percentile** will be the median of the upper 30 data points (31-60). Let me pose the question differently to show that height (and many other measures) cannot be normally distributed, although it can be well approximated as normal. According to the normal distribution, there should be the same proportion of people above the mean as there are below. However, height is >0, whereas it has no maximum (although in reality there could be a limit). So, suppose the mean height is 1.6m, and 0.0001% of the population is 3.3m; if height is normally distributed, then 0.0001% of the population is -0.1m tall, which is not a valid value. The actual % is irrelevant, to the argument.In fact, if you think about the last slide on % response for feelings about math, this MAY be normal ONLY if the mean was 50% and the distribution was unimodal. If the mean isn't 50%, then the distribution is not normal, because no one can answer <0% or >100%.But in many cases, people treat the distributions as approximately normal, because it is sufficient to perform the statistics.To summarize, there's probably no population data that's truly normal, but many are approximately normal (or their means are approximately normal), which in itself is sufficient to describe the data and perform statistical tests.

The numerator for variance is the summation of ***all*** squared deviations.  That means if you have several points the same distance from the mean, each distance is squared and added to the summation.If you have this frequency table:x, Frequency10, 512, 6The mean is ((5 x 10) + (6 x 12)) / (5 + 6)= (50 + 72) / 11 = 122 / 11 = 11.091Denominator of Variance is n - 1 = (5 + 6) - 1 = 11 - 1 = 10Numerator of Variance is summation of all squared distances from mean= (((10 - 11.091)^2) x 5) + (((12 - 11.091)^2) x 6)= (((-1.091)^2) x 5) + (((0.91)^2) x 6)= (1.19 x 5) + (0.826 x 6) = 5.95 + 4.96 = 10.909Divide 10.909 by n - 1 to get Variance = 10.909 / 10 = 1.091Take the square root of the Variance to get standard deviationStd Dev = sqrt(1.091) = 1.044So, you can use this general approach when you have a frequency table. If I tell you that A occurred, that doesn't give you any additional information to predict whether it will rain in Stanford tomorrow! Thus, A & B are independent.But if I tell you that A has occurred, you can say with certainty that ~A has NOT occurred. Sensitivity & Specificity tell about the patients who have not yet undergone the test . So **before doing actual test** , given that patient is non-responder to antibiotic, what's the chance the patient tests positive : **senstivity** ; and **before doing actual test** , given that patient is responder to antibiotic, what's the chance the patient tests negative : **specificity** . On the other hand PPV & NPV tell us about the patients who have undergone the actual test . So **post testing** , given that patient tests positive, what's the chance that the patient is drug resistant : **PPV**. Similarly **post testing** , given that patient tests negative, what's the chance that the patient is drug sensitive : **NPV** . So first two definitions by Violet are correct , and those of PPV & NPV are not.

Laura, your suggesting is like a binary search algorithm. Eg. in video example, if there's 100 people and only 1 person has the disease, then it would only take 7 tests to determine who had it. Test a pool of 50. If negative, look at the other 50; if positive then look at this 50. Test a pool of 25 remaining. If negative ... So 7 tests will get you the one person.The problem becomes if more than 1 person has the disease. One possibility is to shuffle the pools and test them. The number of pools and shuffles would have to be large enough that we could distinguish a single person from another person. Going back to your example, suppose we have 8 people (1-8). Suppose we first pool P1(1,2,3,4) and P2(5,6,7,8) and test both. Now we shuffle the pools so that we have P3(1,2,5,6) and P4(3,4,7,8) and test both. And shuffle again P5(1,5,3,7) and P6(2,4,6,8). Here are our possibilities:If 1 positive -> P1, P3, P5 positiveIf 2 positive -> P1, P3, P6 positiveIf 3 positive -> P1, P4, P5 positiveIf 4 positive -> P1, P4, P6 positiveIf 5 positive -> P2, P3, P5 positiveIf 6 positive -> P2, P3, P6 positiveIf 7 positive -> P2, P4, P5 positiveIf 8 positive -> P2, P4, P6 positiveSo if our test show P1, P2, P4, P6 to be positive, then we know persons 4 and 8 are positive. If P1, P3, P4, P5 show positive, then we know persons 1 and 3 are positive. If P1, P2, P3, P4, P5 positive, then persons 1, 3, 5 and 7 are positive. So in this case, we required 2xlog2(N) tests instead of the log2(N) tests required for the binary search case. So, effectively, we could determine all the positives in a population of 100 by conducting 2xlog2(100) ~ 14 tests regardless of the prevalence of the disease.I think my logic is correct. Type I error occurs when you reject the null hypothesis and the null is actually true. If the null hypothesis is false, then the probability of a type I error is 0. Degrees of freedom tells you how many independent pieces of information you have. So, if you have 100 datapoints but you calculate 1 mean, then you only have 99 degrees of freedom left (if I give you the mean plus any 99 of the datapoints, you can give me the 100th datapoint. So there are only 99 unique pieces of information once you have the mean). To calculate the standard deviation for 1 sample, you have to first calculate one mean so you lose one degree of freedom. To calculate the pooled standard deviation, you must first calculate two means, so you lose 2 standard deviations.

If you have equal sample sizes, the pooled standard deviation will just be the square root of the average variance (second formula posted above). When you have unequal sample sizes, you have to weight each group's contribution by its sample size. The second set of formulas posted above accounts for this weighting.

If you had a woman who dropped out at 6 months, you can't ignore the fact that she was at risk of developing the outcome in question during the 6-month period she was in the study. She could have developed the outcome, but didn't. That means that her data contribute something to the study. If you keep her data in, the overall likelihood of any patient developing the outcome up until the point she dropped out will be lower than if you took her data out (because her contribution make the denominator higher by 1 person). If the study had planned to end at 6 months, you would have been OK with including her data - so it should be no different if she later drops out because her inclusion affects only the data up to 6 months. You can't do clinical studies without patients dropping out, so you have to accommodate that fact rather than ignore it.

Having (I think!) finally understood the Standard Normal (Z) Curve -- (the standard \Bell\" curve) ...with the help of this excellent Stats course I might add, I believe the reason for choosing 1.5 (x IQR) for the whisker can be explained as follows. The area under the central part of the Std N Curve of 50% corresponds to a Z value of -0.67 to +0.67 (ie. 1.34). This \"Z range\" of 1.34 corresponds to the range from the bottom value to the top value of the IQR. Multiply 1.34 by 1.5 gives you 2.01.  Add that to the Z of +0.67 (which corresponds to the top value of the IQR) and you have Z= 2.68 . Plus Minus Z of 2.68 corresponds to 99% of the area under the Std Normal Curve.  Hence anything past the whisker is a real outlier. All much easier to see if you draw out the bell curve.  This I believe explains the logic of choosing 1.5 x IQR for the whisker, by assuming/pretending your data approximates to a Normal distribution."

Thanks for the post! I think the last example of material at the link brings a very good point. As applied to human drug studies, the parallel is that all the humans are very different, and there could be no (or vanishingly small) direct correlation between the fact that you take drug and medical effect. But as you start averaging, and use very large groups of people, you can start seeing trends (even tiny). I guess the conclusion is that the drug is not doing any good for you personally, but is of some merit for public health (financially optimizing national health care budget). Please notice that the bird example has a large number of observation data points analyzed (<zipRedac>0000), so statistical power of such study is big, that's why the trend is visible. To see the effect projected to an individual, smaller studies could be used, say 30 birds observed. In that case the observations could be more related to each individual (or could be simply findings by chance :-)). Less random noise (more correlation) -> you don't need a lot of data in a sample to see the effect! I am not saying <zipRedac>0000 points is worse than 30, it just starts bringing up small details often irrelevant in practice. If you have a systematic component and noise on top of it, you need dampen the noise by multiple averaging, while keeping the systematic portion (in a simplistic homogenous group not affected by averaging). Then if you want to see systematic effect Es, you need to design study with enough of data points to bring Erandom averages below Es to see the effect.At any rate, seeing x-y scatter plot for all the data available is extremely instrumental.

Anaphylaxis can lead to a type of shock (lack of oxygen on a tissue level associated with low blood pressure). In fact, low blood pressure is part of the diagnostic criteria for anaphylaxis. However, low blood pressure is not required to make the diagnosis! Therefore, physicians sometimes use the diagnosis of anaphylactic shock to describe a patient who has hypotension from an allergen. Whereas, anaphylaxis is used to describe an allergic reaction that meets certain criteria but does not include low blood pressure (e.g. rash + respiratory compromise; rash + gastrointestinal compromise). Hope this helps!

Asystole and PEA are not shockable rhythms.  These are treated with medications per ACLS.  Ventricular fibrillation and ventricular tachycardia are shockable rhythms.  Ventricular fibrillation is always pulseless and treated with defibrillation.  Ventricular tachycardia may be present with or without a pulse.  Ventricular tachycardia is treated with defibrillation if the patient is without a pulse.  Ventricular tachycardia is treated with synchronized cardioversion if the patient is unstable and with a pulse.  Ventricular tachycardia can be medically managed if the patient is stable and with a pulse.

Typically, as emergency physicians we do not perform tracheostomies.  These are generally performed by ENT surgeons or general surgeons, and only rarely are done emergently.  In the case of a patient that we, as emergency physicians, are unable to intubate and unable to ventilate, we perform a cricothyrotomy, which is a temporary surgical airway inserted through the cricothyroid membrane.  The anatomy is easier to identify and the procedure is much quicker than a tracheostomy in the crashing patient.
Additionally, the Bougie does not play the same role as an OPA or NPA.

For those that conceptually understand the difference between mutually exclusive and independent events but want to see it make sense mathematically when a certain event [i.e. P(A)=1] and an impossible event [assume P(~A)=0 because A is certain to occur] occur “together,” note that their joint probability will be one [P(A & ~A)=1], not zero. That’s because the probability of such an event happening and not happening is certain; let’s assume that it’s raining right now, then we can be certain that it’s also not not raining [in other words, it's impossible that it's not raining]. Thus, P(A & ~A), which is one, is not equal to P(A) * P(~A), which is zero. This way there is no seeming contradiction, and the events are not independent.Remember, all but for certain events A and ~A can't happen together, but that logic reverses for certain events because they ARE occurring together.

Excellent question. In emergency situations the physician is often forced to act with limited information. You may not know the patient's medical history nor the most likely cause of acute decompensation. In a patient in shock, immediate intervention is required. This often involves plenty of fluids!Remember, however, that there are some excellent clues from the physical exam that can lead you to a quick diagnosis. Just to name a few: hypoxia, shortness of breath and hypotension = obstructive shock from tension pneumothorax (needle the chest!); elevated neck veins, muffled heart sounds = tamponade (pericadiocentesis!); fever and cough with hypotension = combination of distributive and hypovolemic shock from sepsis (lots of fluids and possible vasopressors); shortness of breath, rales, elevated neck veins and worse symptoms with fluids may = cardiogenic shock (ionotropes!)Ultimately, it can become an exercise in trial and error with multiple interventions and reassessment!

As Dr. <redacted> discussed in the video, the data we are dealing with (from the larger sample) is right skewed. If you compare the mean from the 2009 smaller sample and the mean from the 2012 larger sample, you might want to jump to the conclusion that the lead in lipstick increased from 2009 to 2012. This is not correct. We are actually detecting a bigger maximum in the larger sample because we have a right skewed distribution. In the sample of 22, you are less likely to find the extreme values. When you sample more, you are going to see more of the infrequent extreme events. When calculating the mean, you take all the numbers in the dataset, add them together, and divide them by the number of entries. Since your are adding all the numbers, extreme values can influence the mean. With the median, which is the 50% point in the data, infrequent extreme values generally will not impact the value. In this example, we are interested in a value that is representative of our entire sample. The mean is not the best choice because it is influenced by outliers. Hope this helps!Josh

Hello Hany,Let me start with an numerical example.. Say you have:0 0 0 0 1 10 10 10 12 12 12 12 12 12 12 13 13 13 13 13 13 13 13 13 14 14 14 14 14 14 14 14 14 14 14 14 14 14 14 14 14 14 15 15 15  15 15 15 15 15 16 16 16 17 17 17 Do you notice how the \bulk\" of the data has values ranging from 10 to 17? Furthermore, the 0 and 1's look like outliers? The median is the value that lies at the midpoint. In this example, the \"bulk\" of data occurs in the right portion. The \"tail\" extends to the left and contains extremely small values. These small values will pull the mean of the distribution towards the values located at the tail. The mean is calculated using all the data and median is not influenced by the values of the min and max. Picture an image of a skewed distribution in your head (or draw one on a piece of paper). Think of the mean as the balance point of the distribution. In a symmetric distribution, the \"balancing point\" would be in the center. When the data is skewed, you have points that are further away from the balance point, so the center of balance is changed. The mean (center of balance) needs to be pulled in the direction of the skewed data. The median is still just the point that cuts the distribution in half."

HelloGood questions!So it seems like you are confusing cumulative incidence and incidence rate. CI is a proportion, it is the (# people who develop an outcome / # of people initially at risk). With the CI all people are followed for the same amount of time. For example, say you had 40 people in a STATS class and a 1-year period. 14 of these students developed pneumonia. The 1-year cumulative incidence of pneumonia (14/40) or (14/40)*100 = 35 per 100 students. A CI value has no units and the denominator is based on all people who are at risk at risk in the population. It assumes that all people are followed for the same amount of time (in this case a year), and that the population is closed (no people going in or out). Incidence rate (also called incidence density) = # of incident cases / Amount of person time at risk. The best way to think of it is as the occurrence of new cases (of a particular outcome) that arise during a certain amount of person-time of observation. The numerator for CI and incidence rate are exactly the same. The difference is that incidence rate is a true rate because it includes time. In order to understand incidence rate, one needs to talk about person-time. Person-time is only counted up until a person is diagnosed with the outcome of interest. For incidence rate, there is no assumption that everyone is followed for the same amount of time. People can exit and enter the population. So say a person is in a study for 6 months, without getting the outcome, and then drops out - they contribute 6 months to the person time of observation in the candidate population. Say a person is in the study for 12 months, without getting the outcome, and then dies - they contribute 12 months to the person time of observation in the candidate population. Say a person is in the study for 6 months and then gets diagnosed with the outcome of interest - they contribute 6 months to the person time of observation in the candidate population. If these were the only 3 people in the study, the incidence rate would be 1 / 2person-years. The numerator is 1 because 1 person had the outcome and the denominator of the incidence rate is the sum of all the person-times from each member in the candidate population (the population at risk).

Romain, you're working through the course very quickly! Yes, beta coefficients can be a huge source of confusion when authors/readers don't pay close enough attention to the units. Beta coefficients are entirely unit-dependent, so you have to think very carefully about the units. However, they do have some advantages over correlation coefficients. We often want to know how much does Y increase or decrease on average for a 1-unit increase in X. The correlation coefficient doesn't tell us this. A good alternative, for continuous variables, is to standardize them by turning them into Z-scores (Standard Deviation units). If you put standardized variables into the linear regression model, then the beta coefficients will be in SD-Y/SD-X units. So for example, a beta coefficient of 0.25 tells that a 1-SD increase in X correlates to a 0.25-SD increase in Y. It's easier to compare across different predictors if they are all in SD units.

The issue is what we are conditioning on. To calculate the marginal probability of a heads BEFORE the coin flip (not conditioned on the outcome of the coin flip), it is P(H)=0X1/3 + 1/2X1/3 +1X1/3. We need this marginal probability (not conditioned on the outcome) for Bayes' formula: P(HH coin/flipped a heads)=P(flipped a heads/HH coin)*P(HH coin)/P(flipped a heads). In the formula P(flipped a heads) is the marginal probability, which is the probability that we would flip a heads on the first toss (which doesn't depend on the outcome of that toss). Only the conditional probabilities incorporate information about what actually happened.

Hello Hany,I am always happy to help and I appreciate the kind words!Do you just mean left and right skew in general? Let me try explaining both of your questions with one example!As you may have seen in the lectures, a distribution is skewed if one tail is longer than the other (there is a lack of symmetry). With a right skew (also called positive), the bulk (or mass) of the data is on the left and there is a tail extending to the right with extreme values. (Go to google and look a pictures of right skewed data). Do you remember learning about odds ratios? You may remember that Dr. <redacted> mentioned that the sampling distribution of the OR is skewed to the right? If you think about how ORs are calculated and what they mean, it is clear that you cannot have negative values. (A negative OR does not make any sense!). With a limit at the lower end (zero is the limit since it cannot be negative), you get a skewed distribution. An OR can be any positive value from 0 to infinity. With large values on the right...you have right skewed data. So what can you do to ***Transform*** this data to deal with the fact that the distribution is skewed? What happens when you take the log of a negative number (try it on a calculator)?What happens when you take the log of a decimal <1 (for example try 0.5 on a calculator)?What happens when you take the log of 1? (try it on a calculator)?WHat happens when you take the log of 1000? (try it on a calculator)?When you transform data, you replace the variables by a function of the original variable. In many cases, this can change the shape of the distribution. Notice how the log of a large number is a lot smaller (for 1000 you get 6.91)? A logarithmic transformation reduces positive skewness by compressing the right end of the tail and extending the left/lower end. Why does this work?Try ln(1)-ln(.1) = on your calculator...Try ln(10) - ln(1) = on your calculator ...Try ln(1000) - ln(10) = on your calculator...What do you notice? The distance between all of these are the same when you use the log scale! So why use log transformations?Summary: the logarithm can move larger values closer together and smaller values farther apart...which can help with skewed distributions!best,Josh

The standard error is a special case of a standard deviation. Standard deviation measures variability. If we are talking about the variability of a trait, we call it standard deviation. If we are talking about the variability of a statistic (which is a theoretical concept!), we call it a standard error. The standard error helps us to calculate p-values and confidence intervals. The standard deviation of a trait (rather than a statistic) tells us about how much that trait varies in the population.

**Standard deviation** is a measure of variability of **a statistic WITHIN** the sample. D levels, etc.) While standard error (SE) is used to determine the variability of the statistics (SE of the mean fractures, SE of the mean Vit. D, SE of the correlation coefficient between Vit. D levels and No. of fractures).SD has a uniform formula. SE has different formulas for different statistics.

The headlines come from the fact that the lowest quintiles included people running <51 min per week (7 minutes per day), <6 miles , and 1 to 2 times per week. There are of course a lot of caveats! (1) When we break data into quintiles, the sample sizes in each quintile are much smaller than the sample size in the overall study. So chance may play a role. (2) People who run 51 minutes per week are probably not running 5-10 minutes per day; they are probably running 1-2 longer runs of several miles. If you are able to run several miles at once, you are probably reasonably fit and may have been running more than this at other times in your life. (3) People who run a small amount may be participating in many other physical activities; though the authors adjusted for this, it was a very crude adjustment. Glad you are enjoying the course! Every test you run increases the type of a chance I error, so technically you should correct for all p-values at the same time. However, bear in mind that you probably have a lot of overlap between the tests run with Cox regression and those run with logistic regression, for example. They may be so close to measuring the same thing that you are being conservative by adjusting p-values from both methods. So, I'd recommend that you narrow down the number of tests you are running by using clinical judgment. It's unlikely that you need to do both Cox regression and logistic. Pick one outcome that you care most about and focus on that. Also, given the high chance of false positives here, you might try to do some kind of validation.
